j=1,\ldots,k\end{subarray}}\kappa((Z_{i})_{u_{1}v_{1}}^{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,(Z_{i})_{u_{k}v_{k}}^{\alpha_{k}})\,\mathbf{E}\bigg[\frac{\partial^{k}f}{\partial M_{u_{1}v_{1}}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots\partial M_{u_{k}v_{k}}^{\alpha_{k}}}(X(t))\bigg], $$

where $\mathcal{I}:=[d]\times[d]\times\{\mathrm{R},\mathrm{I}\}$ and we denote $M_{uv}^{\mathrm{R}}:=\mathrm{Re}\,M_{uv}$ and $M_{uv}^{\mathrm{I}}:=\mathrm{Im}\,M_{uv}$ . The conclusion follows by applying the second identity of Lemma 4.1 to the cumulant, and using the independence structure of $Z_{ij|\pi}$ to merge the product of expectations in the resulting identity into a single expectation. ∎

The following is the analogous version of Theorem 4.4.

#### Corollary 6.2.

For any $p\geq 3$ and smooth function $f:\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{C}$ we have

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[f(X(t))]=\mbox{}\\
\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=3}^{p-1}\frac{t^{\frac{k}{2}-1}}{(k-1)!}\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}([k])}(-1)^{|\pi|-1}(|\pi|-1)!\,\mathbf{E}\Bigg[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\partial_{Z_{i1|\pi}}\cdots\partial_{Z_{ik|\pi}}f(X(t))\Bigg]+\mathcal{R}, $$

where the remainder term satisfies

$$ |\mathcal{R}|\lesssim\sup_{s,t\in[0,1]}\Bigg\{\Bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\partial_{Z_{i}}^{p}f(X(t,i,s))]\Bigg|+\\
\max_{2\leq k\leq p-1}\Bigg|\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}([k])}\frac{(-1)^{|\pi|-1}(|\pi|-1)!}{(k-1)!}\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\partial_{Z_{i}}^{p-k}\partial_{Z_{i1|\pi}}\cdots\partial_{Z_{ik|\pi}}f(X(t,i,s))]\Bigg|\Bigg\} $$

with $X(t,i,s):=X(t)-(1-s)\sqrt{t}Z_{i}$ .

#### Proof.

The conclusion follows from Theorem 4.4 in exactly the same manner as we derived Corollary 6.1 from Theorem 4.3. ∎

### 6.2. Moments

The aim of this section is to show that the moments $\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2p}]$ are close to their Gaussian analogues $\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}G^{2p}]$ . To this end, we will first compute $\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]$ by means of the cumulant expansion, and then estimate the individual terms to obtain a differential inequality.

We begin by computing the derivatives of the moment function $M\mapsto\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[M^{2p}]$ .

#### Lemma 6.3.

Let $p\in\mathbb{N}$ and $B_{1},\ldots,B_{k}\in\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}$ . Then

$$ \partial_{B_{1}}\cdots\partial_{B_{k}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[M^{2p}]=\mbox{}\\
\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Sym}(k)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r_{1},\ldots,r_{k+1}\geq 0\\
r_{1}+\cdots+r_{k+1}=2p-k\end{subarray}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[M^{r_{1}}B_{\sigma(1)}M^{r_{2}}B_{\sigma(2)}\cdots M^{r_{k}}B_{\sigma(k)}M^{r_{k+1}}]. $$

#### Proof.

This follows by applying the product rule $k$ times. ∎

We will also need the following estimate.

#### Lemma 6.4.

For any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have

$$ \sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}([k])}(|\pi|-1)!\leq 2^{k}(k-1)!. $$

#### Proof.

We first crudely estimate

$$ \sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}([k])}(|\pi|-1)!\leq\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}([k])}(|\pi|-1)!\prod_{J\in\pi}|J|!. $$

Now note that any partition of $[k]$ into $m$ parts can be generated by first choosing $r_{1},\ldots,r_{m}\geq 1$ such that $r_{1}+\cdots+r_{m}=k$ , and then choosing disjoint sets $J_{1},\ldots,J_{m}$ with $|J_{i}|=r_{i}$ . Moreover, each distinct partition is generated precisely $m!$ times in this manner, as relabeling the sets $J_{i}$ does not change the partition. Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}([k])}(|\pi|-1)!\prod_{J\in\pi}|J|! \displaystyle=\sum_{m=1}^{k}(m-1)!\,\frac{1}{m!}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r_{1},\ldots,r_{m}\geq 1\\
r_{1}+\cdots+r_{m}=k\end{subarray}}{k\choose r_{1},\ldots,r_{m}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}r_{j}! \displaystyle=(k-1)!\sum_{m=1}^{k}{k\choose m}=(2^{k}-1)(k-1)!, $$

where the second equality follows as the number of $m$ -tuples of positive integers that sum to $k$ is ${k-1\choose m-1}$ , and the last equality holds by the binomial theorem. ∎

We are now ready to apply the cumulant expansion.

#### Proposition 6.5.

For any $p\in\mathbb{N}$ with $p\geq 2$ , $2p\leq q\leq\infty$ , and $t\in[0,1]$ , we have

$$ \bigg|\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]\bigg|\leq 64p^{3}\max\{R_{q}(X)\sigma_{q}(X)^{2},R_{q}(X)^{3}\}\times\\
\max\big\{\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]^{1-\frac{3}{2p}},(8pR_{q}(X))^{2p-3}\big\}. $$

#### Proof.

Combining Corollary 6.1 and Lemma 6.3 yields

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=3}^{2p}kt^{\frac{k}{2}-1}\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}([k])}(-1)^{|\pi|-1}(|\pi|-1)!\times\mbox{}\\
\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r_{1},\ldots,r_{k+1}\geq 0\\
r_{1}+\cdots+r_{k+1}=2p-k\end{subarray}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{r_{1}}Z_{i1|\pi}X(t)^{r_{2}}Z_{i2|\pi}\cdots X(t)^{r_{k}}Z_{ik|\pi}X(t)^{r_{k+1}}]. $$

Here we used that as $(Z_{i\sigma(j)|\pi})_{i\in[n],j\in[k]}$ and $(Z_{ij|\sigma^{-1}(\pi)})_{i\in[n],j\in[k]}$ have the same distribution for any permutation $\sigma$ , we can eliminate the sum over $\sigma$ in Lemma 6.3 by symmetry. Now let $r=\frac{(2p-k)q}{q-k}$ , so that $2p-k\leq r\leq 2p$ . Let $p_{j}=\frac{r}{r_{j+1}}$ for $j<k$ and $p_{k}=\frac{r}{r_{k+1}+r_{1}}$ . Then we can apply Proposition 5.1 to estimate

$$ \displaystyle\Bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{r_{1}}Z_{i1|\pi}X(t)^{r_{2}}Z_{i2|\pi}\cdots X(t)^{r_{k}}Z_{ik|\pi}X(t)^{r_{k+1}}]\Bigg| \displaystyle\qquad\leq R_{q}(X)^{\frac{(k-2)q}{q-2}}\sigma_{q}(X)^{\frac{2(q-k)}{q-2}}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{r}]^{\frac{2p-k}{r}} \displaystyle\qquad\leq R_{q}(X)^{\frac{(k-2)q}{q-2}}\sigma_{q}(X)^{\frac{2(q-k)}{q-2}}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]^{1-\frac{k}{2p}} $$

for any $r_{1},\ldots,r_{k+1}\geq 0$ with $r_{1}+\cdots+r_{k+1}=2p-k$ . It follows that

$$ \bigg|\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]\bigg|\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=3}^{2p}(4p)^{k}R_{q}(X)^{\frac{(k-2)q}{q-2}}\sigma_{q}(X)^{\frac{2(q-k)}{q-2}}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]^{1-\frac{k}{2p}} $$

using Lemma 6.4, $t\leq 1$ , and that the number of $(k+1)$ -tuples of nonnegative integers that sum to $2p-k$ is ${2p\choose k}\leq\frac{(2p)^{k}}{k!}$ . To simplify the expression, we estimate

$$ \displaystyle\bigg|\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]\bigg| \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=3}^{2p}2^{-k}(8p)^{k}R_{q}(X)^{\frac{(k-2)q}{q-2}}\sigma_{q}(X)^{\frac{2(q-k)}{q-2}}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]^{1-\frac{k}{2p}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{8}\max_{3\leq k\leq 2p}(8p)^{k}R_{q}(X)^{\frac{(k-2)q}{q-2}}\sigma_{q}(X)^{\frac{2(q-k)}{q-2}}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]^{1-\frac{k}{2p}} \displaystyle\leq 64p^{3}\max\big\{R_{q}(X)^{\frac{q}{q-2}}\sigma_{q}(X)^{\frac{2(q-3)}{q-2}}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]^{1-\frac{3}{2p}}, \displaystyle\phantom{\mbox{}\leq 64p^{3}\max\big\{\mbox{}}(8p)^{2p-3}R_{q}(X)^{\frac{(2p-2)q}{q-2}}\sigma_{q}(X)^{\frac{2(q-2p)}{q-2}}\big\}. $$

Here we used that the term inside the maximum on the second line is convex as a function of $k$ , so that the maximum is attained at one of the endpoints $k\in\{3,2p\}$ . The proof is readily concluded using that $R^{\frac{q}{q-2}-1}\sigma^{\frac{2(q-3)}{q-2}}\leq(\max\{R,\sigma\})^{2}$ and $R^{\frac{(2p-2)q}{q-2}-(2p-3)-1}\sigma^{\frac{2(q-2p)}{q-2}}\leq(\max\{R,\sigma\})^{2}$ (as $q\geq 2p\geq 4$ implies that in both cases the exponents on the left-hand side are positive and sum to $2$ ). ∎

It remains to solve the differential inequality in the statement of Proposition 6.5. To this end we will use the following simple lemma.

#### Lemma 6.6.

Let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , $C,K\geq 0$ , and $\alpha\in[0,1]$ . Suppose that

$$ \bigg|\frac{d}{dt}f(t)\bigg|\leq C\max\{f(t)^{1-\alpha},K^{1-\alpha}\} $$

for all $t\in[0,1]$ . Then

$$ |f(1)^{\alpha}-f(0)^{\alpha}|\leq C\alpha+K^{\alpha}. $$

#### Proof.

It follows readily by the chain rule that

$$ \bigg|\frac{d}{dt}(f(t)+K)^{\alpha}\bigg|=\alpha(f(t)+K)^{\alpha-1}\bigg|\frac{d}{dt}f(t)\bigg|\leq C\alpha, $$

so that

$$ |(f(1)+K)^{\alpha}-(f(0)+K)^{\alpha}|=\bigg|\int_{0}^{1}\frac{d}{dt}(f(t)+K)^{\alpha}\,dt\bigg|\leq C\alpha. $$

The conclusion follows as $x^{\alpha}-y^{\alpha}\leq(x+K)^{\alpha}-(y+K)^{\alpha}+K^{\alpha}$ for any $x,y\geq 0$ . ∎

We can now conclude the proof of Theorem 2.9.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.9: first inequality.

If $p=1$ , then $\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]=\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2}]$ is independent of $t$ by construction, and the conclusion is trivial. If $p\geq 2$ , we can apply Lemma 6.6 with $\alpha=\frac{3}{2p}\in[0,1]$ and Proposition 6.5 to obtain

$$ |\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2p}]^{\frac{3}{2p}}-\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}G^{2p}]^{\frac{3}{2p}}|\leq 96p^{2}\max\{R_{q}(X)\sigma_{q}(X)^{2},R_{q}(X)^{3}\}+(8pR_{q}(X))^{3}. $$

The conclusion follows as $|{}x^{\frac{1}{3}}-y^{\frac{1}{3}}|\leq|x-y|^{\frac{1}{3}}$ for $x,y\geq 0$ . ∎

The second inequality of Theorem 2.9 follows by a slight variation of the proof.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.9: second inequality.

Note that $\sigma_{2p}(X)=\sigma_{2p}(X(t))$ for all $t$ , as the definition of $\sigma_{2p}(X)$ depends only on $\mathrm{Cov}(X)$ . We can therefore estimate

$$ \sigma_{2p}(X)^{2p}=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\,(\mathbf{E}[X(t)^{2}]-\mathbf{E}[X(t)]^{2})^{p}\leq\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf{E}[X(t)^{2}]^{p}\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}] $$

for every $t\in[0,1]$ . Here we used that $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}A^{p}\leq\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}B^{p}$ for $B\geq A\geq 0$ , and that $A\mapsto\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}A^{p}$ is convex for $A\geq 0$ [29, Theorem 2.10]. Furthermore, note that

$$ R_{2p}(X)\leq R_{2}(X)^{\frac{q-2p}{p(q-2)}}R_{q}(X)^{\frac{(p-1)q}{p(q-2)}}\leq\sigma_{2p}(X)^{\frac{q-2p}{p(q-2)}}R_{q}(X)^{\frac{(p-1)q}{p(q-2)}} $$

by the Riesz convexity theorem and as $R_{2}(X)=\sigma_{2}(X)\leq\sigma_{2p}(X)$ . Consequently, we can bound the differential inequality in the proof of Proposition 6.5 as

$$ \displaystyle\bigg|\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]\bigg| \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=3}^{2p}(4p)^{k}R_{2p}(X)^{\frac{(k-2)p}{p-1}}\sigma_{2p}(X)^{\frac{2p-k}{p-1}}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]^{1-\frac{k}{2p}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=3}^{2p}(4p)^{k}R_{q}(X)^{\frac{(k-2)q}{q-2}}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]^{1-\frac{k}{2p}+\frac{q-k}{p(q-2)}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{8}\max_{3\leq k\leq 2p}(8p)^{k}R_{q}(X)^{\frac{(k-2)q}{q-2}}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]^{1-\frac{k}{2p}+\frac{q-k}{p(q-2)}}. $$

By convexity, we may bound all terms in the maximum by their value at either $k=2+\frac{q-2}{q}\leq 3$ or $k=2+2p\frac{q-2}{q}\geq 2p$ , so that

$$ \bigg|\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]\bigg|\leq\frac{(8p)^{2+\frac{q-2}{q}}R_{q}(X)}{8}\max\big\{\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X(t)^{2p}]^{1-\frac{1}{2p}},\big((8p)^{\frac{q-2}{q}}R_{q}(X)\big)^{2p-1}\big\}. $$

The conclusion follows from Lemma 6.6. ∎

#### Remark 6.7.

That there is considerable room in the proof of Theorem 2.9 is evident from the crude inequality in the first equation display of the proof of Lemma 6.4. This additional room can be used to capture models whose summands $Z_{i}$ are not uniformly bounded, but have subexponential tails. For the purposes of this paper, such an extension is not needed as the truncation method that will be developed in section 8 below yields far more general results. However, this extra room can be of significant utility in extending the approach of this paper to random matrices that are not captured by the independent sum model (2.1), cf. [63].

### 6.3. Resolvent moments

The aim of this section is to prove the following universality principle for the moments of the resolvent. This result will form the basis for the proof of Theorem 2.6 (which is given in section 7 below).

#### Theorem 6.8 (Resolvent moments universality).

We have

$$ \big|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X|^{-2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}-\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-G|^{-2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\big|\lesssim\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}p^{2}+R(X)^{3}p^{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}} $$

for any $p\in\mathbb{N}$ and $z\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,z>0$ .

The proof of Theorem 6.8 is very similar in spirit to that of Theorem 2.9. However, as the resolvent is not a polynomial (and does not have a globally convergent power series), we must truncate the cumulant expansion as in Corollary 6.2.

We begin by computing the derivatives of $M\mapsto\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-M|^{-2p}$ .

#### Lemma 6.9.

Let $z\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,z>0$ , $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , and $M,B_{1},\ldots,B_{k}\in\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}$ . Denote the resolvent of $M$ as $\mathrm{R}_{M}(z):=(z\mathbf{1}-M)^{-1}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{B_{1}}\cdots\partial_{B_{k}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-M|^{-2p}=\mbox{} \displaystyle\quad\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Sym}(k)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,m\geq 0\\
l+m=k\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r_{1},\ldots,r_{l+1}\geq 1\\
r_{1}+\cdots+r_{l+1}=p+l\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s_{1},\ldots,s_{m+1}\geq 1\\
s_{1}+\cdots+s_{m+1}=p+m\end{subarray}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[\mathrm{R}_{M}(z)^{r_{1}}B_{\sigma(1)} \displaystyle\quad\qquad\cdots\mathrm{R}_{M}(z)^{r_{l}}B_{\sigma(l)}\mathrm{R}_{M}(z)^{r_{l+1}}\mathrm{R}_{M}(\bar{z})^{s_{1}}B_{\sigma(l+1)}\cdots\mathrm{R}_{M}(\bar{z})^{s_{m}}B_{\sigma(k)}\mathrm{R}_{M}(\bar{z})^{s_{m+1}}]. $$

In particular,

$$ \big|\partial_{B_{1}}\cdots\partial_{B_{k}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-M|^{-2p}\big|\leq\frac{(2p-1+k)!}{(2p-1)!}\frac{\|B_{1}\|_{k}\cdots\|B_{k}\|_{k}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2p+k}}. $$

#### Proof.

The identity follows by applying the product rule $k$ times to $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-M|^{-2p}=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[\mathrm{R}_{M}(z)^{p}\mathrm{R}_{M}(\bar{z})^{p}]$ and using that $\partial_{B}\mathrm{R}_{M}(z)=\mathrm{R}_{M}(z)B\mathrm{R}_{M}(z)$ . To prove the inequality, note that each summand is bounded by $(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{-2p-k}\|B_{1}\|_{k}\cdots\|B_{k}\|_{k}$ by Hölder’s inequality and $\|\mathrm{R}_{M}(z)\|\leq|\mathrm{Im}\,z|^{-1}$ , while the sums have $\frac{(2p-1+k)!}{(2p-1)!}$ terms (the latter is most easily seen by applying the first identity with $d=1$ .) ∎

We can now apply the cumulant expansion.

#### Proposition 6.10.

For any $z\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,z>0$ , $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , and $t\in[0,1]$ , we have

$$ \bigg|\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p}]\bigg|\\
\lesssim\frac{p^{3}R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}}\max\Bigg\{\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p}]^{1-\frac{1}{2p}},\frac{(32pR(X))^{6p-3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{8p-4}}\Bigg\}. $$

#### Proof.

Combining Corollary 6.2 with Lemma 6.9 yields

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p}]=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=3}^{6p-1}kt^{\frac{k}{2}-1}\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}([k])}(-1)^{|\pi|-1}(|\pi|-1)!\times\mbox{} \displaystyle\enskip\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,m\geq 0\\
l+m=k\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r_{1},\ldots,r_{l+1}\geq 1\\
r_{1}+\cdots+r_{l+1}=p+l\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s_{1},\ldots,s_{m+1}\geq 1\\
s_{1}+\cdots+s_{m+1}=p+m\end{subarray}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(z)^{r_{1}}Z_{i1|\pi}\cdots\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(z)^{r_{l}}Z_{il|\pi}\cdot\mbox{} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\quad\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(z)^{r_{l+1}}\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(\bar{z})^{s_{1}}Z_{i(l+1)|\pi}\cdots\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(\bar{z})^{s_{m}}Z_{ik|\pi}\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(\bar{z})^{s_{m+1}}]+\mathcal{R} $$

with

$$ |\mathcal{R}|\lesssim\frac{(8p-1)!}{(2p-1)!}\frac{2^{6p}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{8p}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Z_{i}^{6p}]. $$

Here we eliminated the sum over permutations $\sigma$ in the identity as in the proof of Proposition 6.5, and we used Lemma 6.4 and Hölder’s inequality in the estimate of the remainder. To proceed, we apply Proposition 5.1 with $p_{j}=\frac{2p+k}{r_{j+1}}$ for $1\leq j<l$ , $p_{l}=\frac{2p+k}{r_{l+1}+s_{1}}$ , $p_{j}=\frac{2p+k}{s_{j-l+1}}$ for $l<j<k$ , $p_{k}=\frac{2p+k}{s_{m+1}+r_{1}}$ , and $q=\infty$ to estimate

$$ \displaystyle\Bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(z)^{r_{1}}Z_{i1|\pi}\cdots\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(z)^{r_{l}}Z_{il|\pi}\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(z)^{r_{l+1}}\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(\bar{z})^{s_{1}}Z_{i(l+1)|\pi} \displaystyle\qquad\quad\cdots\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(\bar{z})^{s_{m}}Z_{ik|\pi}\mathrm{R}_{X(t)}(\bar{z})^{s_{m+1}}]\Bigg|\leq R(X)^{k-2}\sigma(X)^{2}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p-k}]. $$

We can therefore estimate

$$ \bigg|\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p}]\bigg|\leq C\frac{(8p-1)!}{(2p-1)!}\frac{2^{6p}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{8p}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Z_{i}^{6p}]\\
+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=3}^{6p-1}\frac{(2p-1+k)!}{(2p-1)!}2^{k}R(X)^{k-2}\sigma(X)^{2}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p-k}] $$

for a universal constant $C$ , where we used Lemma 6.4 and that the sums over $l,m,r_{j},s_{j}$ contain a total of ${2p-1+k\choose 2p-1}$ terms (cf. the proof of Lemma 6.9). Thus

$$ \bigg|\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p}]\bigg|\leq C\frac{(16p)^{6p}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{8p}}R(X)^{6p-2}\sigma(X)^{2}\\
+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=3}^{6p-1}(16p)^{k}R(X)^{k-2}\sigma(X)^{2}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p-k}], $$

where we used $\frac{(2p-1+k)!}{(2p-1)!}\leq(8p)^{k}$ for $k\leq 6p$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Z_{i}^{6p}]\leq R(X)^{6p-2}\sigma(X)^{2}$ .

We now proceed as in the proof of Proposition 6.5. As the terms inside the sum are convex as a function of $k$ , we can estimate

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=3}^{6p-1}(16p)^{k}R(X)^{k-2}\sigma(X)^{2}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p-k}] \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{8}\max\big\{(32p)^{3}R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p-3}], \displaystyle\phantom{\mbox{}\leq\frac{1}{8}\max\big\{\mbox{}}(32p)^{6p}R(X)^{6p-2}\sigma(X)^{2}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-8p}]\big\} \displaystyle\leq\frac{(32p)^{3}R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}}{8(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}}\max\Bigg\{\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p}]^{1-\frac{1}{2p}},\frac{(32pR(X))^{6p-3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{8p-4}}\Bigg\}, $$

where we used that $\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p+1}]\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-X(t)|^{-2p}]^{1-\frac{1}{2p}}$ by Jensen’s inequality, and that $\|(z\mathbf{1}-X(t))^{-1}\|\leq(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{-1}$ . The conclusion follows readily. ∎

The proof of Theorem 6.8 is now immediate.

#### Proof of Theorem 6.8.

Combine Proposition 6.10 and Lemma 6.6. ∎

### 6.4. Resolvent matrix

The aim of this section is to prove the resolvent universality principle of Theorem 2.10. In contrast to the universality principles for the moments and resolvent moments, the present result is much more classical in nature as its proof does not require the cumulant expansion; it could therefore also be approached by means of more traditional universality methods as in [32, 33]. In particular, we will apply Corollary 6.2 with $p=3$ : in this special case, the proof of Corollary 6.2 uses only Taylor expansion and no cumulants appear.

Nonetheless, the present situation is somewhat different in nature than the previous universality results in that we bound the difference between the expected resolvents of $X$ and $G$ in norm (as opposed to their traces, see Remark 6.13 below). This introduces some additional subtleties that must be addressed in the proof.

We begin by applying Corollary 6.2 in the present setting.

#### Lemma 6.11.

We have

$$ \big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}]\big\|\lesssim\bigg(\frac{R(X)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}}+\frac{R(X)^{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{6}}\bigg)\mathbf{E}\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{i}^{2}\Bigg\|. $$

#### Proof.

We readily compute

$$ \partial_{B_{1}}\partial_{B_{2}}\partial_{B_{3}}(z\mathbf{1}-M)^{-1}=\mbox{}\\
\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Sym}(3)}(z\mathbf{1}-M)^{-1}B_{\sigma(1)}(z\mathbf{1}-M)^{-1}B_{\sigma(2)}(z\mathbf{1}-M)^{-1}B_{\sigma(3)}(z\mathbf{1}-M)^{-1}. $$

Applying Corollary 6.2 to $f(M)=\langle v,(z\mathbf{1}-M)^{-1}w\rangle$ with $p=3$ yields

$$ \big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}]\big\|=\sup_{\|v\|=\|w\|=1}\bigg|\int_{0}^{1}\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\langle v,(z\mathbf{1}-X(t))^{-1}w\rangle]\,dt\bigg|\\
\lesssim F(Z,Z,Z)+F(Z,Z^{\prime},Z^{\prime})+F(Z^{\prime},Z,Z^{\prime})+F(Z^{\prime},Z^{\prime},Z), $$

where $Z^{\prime}=(Z_{i}^{\prime})_{1\leq i\leq n}$ is an independent copy of $Z=(Z_{i})_{1\leq i\leq n}$ ,

$$ F(Z^{(1)},Z^{(2)},Z^{(3)})=\sup_{\|v\|=\|w\|=1}\sup_{s,t\in[0,1]}\Bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\langle v,\mathrm{R}_{tis}Z_{i}^{(1)}\mathrm{R}_{tis}Z_{i}^{(2)}\mathrm{R}_{tis}Z_{i}^{(3)}\mathrm{R}_{tis}w\rangle]\Bigg|, $$

and $\mathrm{R}_{tis}=(z\mathbf{1}-X(t,i,s))^{-1}$ with $X(t,i,s)=X(t)-(1-s)\sqrt{t}Z_{i}$ . (Note that the term with $|\pi|=2$ in the bound on $|\mathcal{R}|$ in Corollary 6.2 vanishes as $\mathbf{E}[Z_{i}]=0$ .)

As $\|\mathrm{R}_{tis}\|\leq(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{-1}$ and $\|Z_{i}\|\leq R(X)$ , we have

$$ F(Z^{(1)},Z^{(2)},Z^{(3)})\leq\frac{R(X)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}\sup_{\|v\|=\|w\|=1}\sup_{s,t\in[0,1]}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\|Z_{i}^{(1)}\mathrm{R}_{tis}^{*}v\|\|Z_{i}^{(3)}\mathrm{R}_{tis}w\|]. $$

Now note that as $A^{-1}-B^{-1}=A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{R}_{tis} \displaystyle=\mathrm{R}_{t}-(1-s)\sqrt{t}\,\mathrm{R}_{tis}Z_{i}\mathrm{R}_{t}, \displaystyle\mathrm{R}_{tis}^{*} \displaystyle=\mathrm{R}_{t}^{*}-(1-s)\sqrt{t}\,\mathrm{R}_{tis}Z_{i}\mathrm{R}_{t}^{*} $$

with $\mathrm{R}_{t}=(z\mathbf{1}-X(t))^{-1}$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle\|Z_{i}^{(3)}\mathrm{R}_{tis}w\| \displaystyle\leq\|Z_{i}^{(3)}\mathrm{R}_{t}w\|+\frac{R(X)}{\mathrm{Im}\,z}\|Z_{i}\mathrm{R}_{t}w\|, \displaystyle\|Z_{i}^{(1)}\mathrm{R}_{tis}^{*}v\| \displaystyle\leq\|Z_{i}^{(1)}\mathrm{R}_{t}^{*}v\|+\frac{R(X)}{\mathrm{Im}\,z}\|Z_{i}\mathrm{R}_{t}^{*}v\| $$

for $s,t\in[0,1]$ . Using $(a+b)(c+d)\leq a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}$ yields

$$ \mathbf{E}[\|Z_{i}^{(1)}\mathrm{R}_{tis}^{*}v\|\|Z_{i}^{(3)}\mathrm{R}_{tis}w\|]\leq\mathbf{E}[\langle\mathrm{R}_{t}w,(Z_{i}^{(3)})^{2}\mathrm{R}_{t}w\rangle]+\mathbf{E}[\langle\mathrm{R}_{t}^{*}v,(Z_{i}^{(1)})^{2}\mathrm{R}_{t}^{*}v\rangle]+\\
\frac{R(X)^{2}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}\big(\mathbf{E}[\langle\mathrm{R}_{t}w,Z_{i}^{2}\mathrm{R}_{t}w\rangle]+\mathbf{E}[\langle\mathrm{R}_{t}^{*}v,Z_{i}^{2}\mathrm{R}_{t}^{*}v\rangle]\big). $$

We can therefore estimate

$$ F(Z^{(1)},Z^{(2)},Z^{(3)})\lesssim\bigg(\frac{R(X)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}}+\frac{R(X)^{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{6}}\bigg)\mathbf{E}\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{i}^{2}\Bigg\| $$

whenever $Z^{(k)}$ have the same distribution as $Z$ , concluding the proof. ∎

We also need the following simple lemma.

#### Lemma 6.12.

We have

$$ \mathbf{E}\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{i}^{2}\Bigg\|\lesssim\sigma(X)^{2}+R(X)^{2}\log d. $$

#### Proof.

We can estimate

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{E}\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{i}^{2}\Bigg\| \displaystyle\leq\sigma(X)^{2}+\mathbf{E}\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Z_{i}^{2}-\mathbf{E}Z_{i}^{2})\Bigg\| \displaystyle\lesssim\sigma(X)^{2}+\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[(Z_{i}^{2}-\mathbf{E}Z_{i}^{2})^{2}]\Bigg\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{\log d}+R(X)^{2}\log d \displaystyle\lesssim\sigma(X)^{2}+R(X)\sigma(X)\sqrt{\log d}+R(X)^{2}\log d, $$

where the second line follows from the matrix Bernstein inequality (1.3). The conclusion follows as $R(X)\sigma(X)\sqrt{\log d}\leq\sigma(X)^{2}+R(X)^{2}\log d$ . ∎

We can now complete the proof of Theorem 2.10.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.10.

Lemmas 6.11 and 6.12 yield

$$ \big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}]\big\|\lesssim\frac{\sigma(X)^{2}+R(X)^{2}\log d}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}\bigg(\frac{R(X)}{\mathrm{Im}\,z}+\frac{R(X)^{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}\bigg). $$

This yields the first inequality of Theorem 2.10 when $\mathrm{Im}\,z\geq R(X)$ . On the other hand, when $\mathrm{Im}\,z<R(X)$ , we can crudely estimate

$$ \displaystyle\big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}]\big\| \displaystyle\leq\big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]\big\|+\big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}]\big\| \displaystyle\leq\frac{2}{\mathrm{Im}\,z}\leq\frac{2R(X)^{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}}, $$

concluding the proof of the first inequality.

To prove the second inequality, it suffices to consider real-valued $\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ (as otherwise we may apply the real-valued inequality separately to the real and imaginary parts of $\varphi$ ). Then $\varphi(X)$ and $\varphi(G)$ are self-adjoint, so we may express

$$ \displaystyle\big\|\mathbf{E}[\varphi(X)]-\mathbf{E}[\varphi(G)]\big\| \displaystyle=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\big|\langle v,\mathbf{E}[\varphi(X)]v\rangle-\langle v,\mathbf{E}[\varphi(G)]v\rangle\big| \displaystyle=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\bigg|\int\varphi\,d\mu_{v}-\int\varphi\,d\nu_{v}\bigg| $$

where we defined the probability measures $\mu_{v},\nu_{v}$ for $\|v\|=1$ so that $\int\varphi\,d\mu_{v}=\langle v,\mathbf{E}[\varphi(X)]v\rangle$ and $\int\varphi\,d\nu_{v}=\langle v,\mathbf{E}[\varphi(G)]v\rangle$ for all bounded continuous $\varphi$ . As the first inequality of Theorem 2.10 implies that

$$ \sup_{\|v\|=1}\bigg|\int\frac{1}{z-x}\,\mu_{v}(dx)-\int\frac{1}{z-x}\,\nu_{v}(dx)\bigg|\lesssim\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}+R(X)^{3}\log d}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}}, $$

the second inequality of Theorem 2.10 follows from [9, Lemma 5.11]. ∎

#### Remark 6.13 (An improved inequality for Stieltjes transforms).

The main complication in the proof of Theorem 2.10 arises from the fact that we aim to achieve a norm estimate. If we are only interested in establishing universality of the trace of the resolvent (that is, of the Stieltjes transform of the empirical spectral distribution), the proof simplifies greatly and yields a better bound. Indeed, the first equation display of the proof of Lemma 6.11 and Hölder’s inequality readily yield

$$ |\mathbf{E}[\partial_{Y_{1}}\partial_{Y_{2}}\partial_{Y_{3}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mbox{}(z\mathbf{1}-X(t,i,s))^{-1}]|\leq\frac{6\|Y_{1}\|_{3}\|Y_{2}\|_{3}\|Y_{3}\|_{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}} $$

for any random matrices $Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3}$ . Combining this inequality with the $p=3$ case of Corollary 6.2 immediately yields the estimate

$$ |\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}]|\lesssim\frac{1}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|Z_{i}|^{3}]. $$

In particular, in this case the logarithmic dimension dependence is eliminated.

## 7. Universality of the spectrum

The aim of this section is to prove Theorem 2.6 and Corollary 2.7. The main idea behind the proof is that universality of the spectrum can be deduced from the bound on the moments of the resolvent in Theorem 6.8 using a technique that was developed for Gaussian random matrices in [9, §6.2]. The difficulty in the present setting is that the resolvent of the non-Gaussian random matrix $X$ exhibits more complicated concentration properties than in the Gaussian case.

We first introduce some basic estimates in section 7.1. In sections 7.2 and 7.3, we bound the probability that $\mathrm{sp}(X)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(G)+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ and $\mathrm{sp}(G)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(X)+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ , respectively. Combining these bounds yields the Hausdorff distance bound of Theorem 2.6. Finally, Corollary 2.7 will be proved in section 7.4.

### 7.1. Preliminaries

The basic principle behind the proof is the following deterministic lemma, which is a trivial modification of [9, Lemma 6.4].

#### Lemma 7.1.

Let $C,K_{1},K_{2},K_{3}\geq 0$ , and let $A,B\in\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}$ satisfy

$$ \|(z\mathbf{1}-A)^{-1}\|\leq C\|(z\mathbf{1}-B)^{-1}\|+\frac{K_{1}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+\frac{K_{2}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}+\frac{K_{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}} $$

for all $z=\lambda+i\varepsilon$ with $\lambda\in\mathrm{sp}(A)$ and $\varepsilon=6K_{1}\vee(6K_{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}\vee(6K_{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}$ . Then

$$ \mathrm{sp}(A)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(B)+2C\varepsilon[-1,1]. $$

#### Proof.

Fix $\lambda\in\mathrm{sp}(A)$ and $z=\lambda+i\varepsilon$ , where $\varepsilon$ is as defined in the statement. As $\|(z\mathbf{1}-A)^{-1}\|=(\mathrm{dist}(z,\mathrm{sp}(A)))^{-1}$ , the assumption implies that

$$ \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\leq\frac{C}{\sqrt{\varepsilon^{2}+\mathrm{dist}(\lambda,\mathrm{sp}(B))^{2}}}+\frac{K_{1}}{\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{K_{2}}{\varepsilon^{3}}+\frac{K_{3}}{\varepsilon^{4}}. $$

If $\mathrm{dist}(\lambda,\mathrm{sp}(B))>2C\varepsilon$ , we would have $\frac{1}{2}<\frac{K_{1}}{\varepsilon}+\frac{K_{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{K_{3}}{\varepsilon^{3}}\leq\frac{1}{2}$ by the definition of $\varepsilon$ , which is impossible. Thus $\mathrm{dist}(\lambda,\mathrm{sp}(B))\leq 2C\varepsilon$ for all $\lambda\in\mathrm{sp}(A)$ . ∎

The main idea behind the proof of Theorem 2.6 is that we will engineer the assumption of Lemma 7.1 by using Theorem 6.8 and concentration of measure. Before we turn to the details of the argument, let us prove a crude a priori bound on the spectrum that will be needed below.

#### Lemma 7.2.

We have

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{sp}(X)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(\mathbf{E}X)+C\{\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{d+t}+R(X)(d+t)\}[-1,1]\big]\geq 1-e^{-t} $$

and

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{sp}(G)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(\mathbf{E}G)+C\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{d+t}\,[-1,1]\big]\geq 1-e^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq 0$ , where $C$ is a universal constant.

#### Proof.

Let $N\subset\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ be a $\frac{1}{4}$ -net of the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}:=\{x\in\mathbb{C}^{d}:\|x\|=1\}$ , that is, $\mathrm{dist}(x,N)\leq\frac{1}{4}$ for all $x\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ . A routine estimate [75, p. 110] yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{P}[\|X-\mathbf{E}X\|\geq x] \displaystyle\leq\mathbf{P}\bigg[\max_{v,w\in N}|\langle v,(X-\mathbf{E}X)w\rangle|\geq\frac{x}{4}\bigg] \displaystyle\leq|N|^{2}\sup_{v,w\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}\mathbf{P}\bigg[|\langle v,(X-\mathbf{E}X)w\rangle|\geq\frac{x}{4}\bigg]. $$

By viewing $\mathbb{C}^{d}$ as a $2d$ -dimensional real vector space, we may use a standard volume argument [75, Lemma 2.3.4] to choose the net $N$ so that $|N|\leq C^{d}$ for a universal constant $C$ . On the other hand, by Bernstein’s inequality [22, Theorem 2.10]

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{P}\big[|\langle v,(X-\mathbf{E}X)w\rangle|\geq 2\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2}R(X)x\big] \displaystyle\qquad\leq\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\Bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Re}\,\langle v,Z_{i}w\rangle\Bigg|\geq\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{2x}+R(X)x\Bigg] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\Bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Im}\,\langle v,Z_{i}w\rangle\Bigg|\geq\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{2x}+R(X)x\Bigg]\leq 4e^{-x} $$

for all $x\geq 0$ and $v,w\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ . Combining the above estimates yields

$$ \mathbf{P}[\|X-\mathbf{E}X\|\geq 8\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{cd+t}+4\sqrt{2}R(X)(cd+t)]\leq C^{2d}e^{-cd-t}\leq e^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq 0$ , provided the universal constant $c$ is chosen sufficiently large. The first inequality in the statement now follows by noting that

$$ \mathrm{sp}(X)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(\mathbf{E}X)+\|X-\mathbf{E}X\|[-1,1] $$

by Weyl’s inequality $\max_{i}|\lambda_{i}(A)-\lambda_{i}(B)|\leq\|A-B\|$ for self-adjoint matrices $A,B$ [18, Corollary III.2.6] (here $\lambda_{i}(A)$ is the $i$ th largest eigenvalue of $A$ ).

The inequality for the Gaussian matrix $G$ follows in the identical fashion, except that we replace Bernstein’s inequality by the Gaussian bound

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[|\langle v,(G-\mathbf{E}G)w\rangle|\geq 2\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{x}\big]\leq 4e^{-x} $$

(this follows from the Gaussian tail bound [22, p. 22] as the real and imaginary parts of $\langle v,(G-\mathbf{E}G)w\rangle$ are Gaussian variables with variance bounded by $\sigma_{*}(X)^{2}$ ). ∎

### 7.2. Proof of Theorem 2.6: upper bound

The aim of the present section is to prove that $\mathrm{sp}(X)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(G)+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ with high probability for a suitable choice of $\varepsilon$ . This will be accomplished by showing that the corresponding resolvent norm inequality of Lemma 7.1 holds with with high probability.

We begin by showing that this is the case for a single choice of $z$ . Note that the joint distribution of $X$ and $G$ is irrelevant to the following proofs.

#### Lemma 7.3.

Let $z\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,z>0$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{P}\bigg[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\| \displaystyle\geq C\bigg\{\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|+\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}\sqrt{x} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\mbox{}+\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}x^{2}+R(X)^{3}x^{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}}\bigg\}\bigg]\leq 3e^{-x} $$

for all $x\geq\log d$ , where $C$ is a universal constant.

#### Proof.

We begin by noting that Markov’s inequality implies

$$ \mathbf{P}\Big[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|\geq e\,\mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\Big]\leq e^{-2p}. $$

By Theorem 6.8, the expectation inside the probability satisfies

$$ \mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\leq d^{\frac{1}{2p}}\mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}+Cd^{\frac{1}{2p}}\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}p^{2}+R(X)^{3}p^{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}} $$

for $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , where $C$ is a universal constant. Here we used that $\frac{1}{d}\|A\|\leq\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}A\leq\|A\|$ for any positive semidefinite matrix $A\in\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}$ .

To proceed, note first that Lemma 5.5 implies

$$ \mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\leq\mathbf{E}\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|+C\sqrt{p}\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}} $$

for $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , where $C$ is a universal constant (this follows as the $L^{p}$ -norm of a $\sigma^{2}$ -subgaussian random variable is at most of order $\sigma\sqrt{p}$ , cf. [22, Theorem 2.1]). Another application of Lemma 5.5 therefore yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\bigg[\mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\geq\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|+C_{1}\sqrt{p}\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}\bigg]\leq 2e^{-C_{2}p} $$

for $p\in\mathbb{N}$ and universal constants $C_{1},C_{2}$ .

Combining the above bounds yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{P}\bigg[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\| \displaystyle\geq ed^{\frac{1}{2p}}\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|+C_{1}ed^{\frac{1}{2p}}\sqrt{p}\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}} \displaystyle\qquad\mbox{}+Ced^{\frac{1}{2p}}\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}p^{2}+R(X)^{3}p^{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}}\bigg]\leq e^{-2p}+2e^{-C_{2}p} $$

for $p\in\mathbb{N}$ . The conclusion follows readily using $d^{\frac{1}{2p}}\leq e^{\frac{1}{2}}$ for $p\geq\log d$ . ∎

We are now ready to prove one direction of Theorem 2.6.

#### Proposition 7.4.

For any $t\geq 0$ , we have

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{sp}(X)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(G)+C\varepsilon(t)[-1,1]\big]\geq 1-de^{-t}, $$

where $C$ is a universal constant and $\varepsilon(t)$ is as defined in Theorem 2.6.

#### Proof.

Define the set

$$ \Omega_{x}:=\mathrm{sp}(\mathbf{E}X)+C^{\prime}\{\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{d+x}+R(X)(d+x)\}[-1,1], $$

where $C^{\prime}$ is the universal constant of Lemma 7.2. Then $\Omega_{x}$ is a union of $d$ intervals of length $2C^{\prime}\{\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{d+x}+R(X)(d+x)\}$ . We can therefore find $\mathcal{N}_{x}\subset\Omega_{x}$ with $|\mathcal{N}_{x}|\leq\frac{4C^{\prime}d(d+x)}{x}$ such that each $\lambda\in\Omega_{x}$ satisfies $\mathrm{dist}(\lambda,\mathcal{N}_{x})\leq\sigma_{*}\sqrt{x}+R(X)x$ . In particular, for every $\lambda\in\Omega_{x}$ , there exists $\lambda^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}_{x}$ so that

$$ \big|\|((\lambda+i\varepsilon)\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|-\|((\lambda^{\prime}+i\varepsilon)\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|\big|\leq\frac{\sigma_{*}\sqrt{x}+R(X)x}{\varepsilon^{2}} $$

as well as the analogous bound where $X$ is replaced by $G$ (here we used the identity $A^{-1}-B^{-1}=A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1}$ ). We can therefore estimate

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{P}\bigg[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|\geq C\bigg\{\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|+\frac{3\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{x}+2R(X)x}{\varepsilon^{2}} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\mbox{}+\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}x^{2}+R(X)^{3}x^{3}}{\varepsilon^{4}}\bigg\}\mbox{ for some }z\in\mathrm{sp}(X)+i\varepsilon\bigg] \displaystyle\leq\mathbf{P}\bigg[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|\geq C\bigg\{\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|+\frac{3\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{x}+2R(X)x}{\varepsilon^{2}} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\mbox{}+\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}x^{2}+R(X)^{3}x^{3}}{\varepsilon^{4}}\bigg\}\mbox{ for some }z\in\Omega_{x}+i\varepsilon\bigg]+e^{-x} \displaystyle\leq\mathbf{P}\bigg[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|\geq C\bigg\{\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|+\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\sqrt{x} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\mbox{}+\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}x^{2}+R(X)^{3}x^{3}}{\varepsilon^{4}}\bigg\}\mbox{ for some }z\in\mathcal{N}_{x}+i\varepsilon\bigg]+e^{-x} \displaystyle\leq(3|\mathcal{N}_{x}|+1)e^{-x}\leq\bigg(1+\frac{12C^{\prime}d(d+x)}{x}\bigg)e^{-x} $$

for $x\geq\log d$ , where we used Lemma 7.2 in the first inequality and a union bound and Lemma 7.3 in the third inequality (here $C>1$ is the constant of Lemma 7.3).

Now let $x=Lt$ for a universal constant $L$ . Recalling the standing assumption $d\geq 2$ , it is readily seen that we may choose $L>1$ sufficiently large so that

$$ \bigg(1+\frac{12C^{\prime}d(d+x)}{x}\bigg)e^{-x}\leq de^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq\log d$ . Then we have shown that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{P}\bigg[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|\leq 3L^{3}C\bigg\{\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|+\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{t}+R(X)t}{\varepsilon^{2}} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\mbox{}+\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}t^{2}+R(X)^{3}t^{3}}{\varepsilon^{4}}\bigg\}\mbox{ for all }z\in\mathrm{sp}(X)+i\varepsilon\bigg]\geq 1-de^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq\log d$ . On the other hand, the same bound holds trivially for $t<\log d$ as then $1-de^{-t}<0$ . The proof is concluded by applying Lemma 7.1. ∎

### 7.3. Proof of Theorem 2.6: lower bound

We now turn to the complementary inequality $\mathrm{sp}(G)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(X)+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ with high probability. The proof is similar in spirit to that of the upper bound, but we must now work with the more complicated concentration inequality of Proposition 5.6. As before, we begin by establishing a resolvent norm inequality for a single choice of $z$ .

#### Lemma 7.5.

Let $z\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,z>0$ . Then

$$ \mathbf{P}\bigg[\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|\geq C\bigg\{\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|+\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)x+R(X)^{2}x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}+\mbox{}\\
\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}x^{2}+R(X)^{3}x^{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}}+\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)x^{\frac{1}{2}}+R(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}x^{\frac{3}{4}}+R(X)x}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}\bigg\}\bigg]\leq 3e^{-x} $$

for all $x\geq\log d$ , where $C$ is a universal constant.

#### Proof.

As in the proof of Lemma 7.3, we have

$$ \mathbf{P}\Big[\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|\geq e\,\mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\Big]\leq e^{-2p} $$

and

$$ \mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\leq d^{\frac{1}{2p}}\mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}+Cd^{\frac{1}{2p}}\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}p^{2}+R(X)^{3}p^{3}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}} $$

for $p\in\mathbb{N}$ by Markov’s inequality and Theorem 6.8.

To proceed, we use that Proposition 5.6 implies

$$ \mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\leq\mathbf{E}\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|+C\bigg\{\frac{R(X)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+\frac{R(X)^{2}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}\bigg\}\,p\\
+C\bigg\{\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)+R(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{E}\|X-\mathbf{E}X\|)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+\frac{R(X)(\mathbf{E}\|X-\mathbf{E}X\|^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}\bigg\}\sqrt{p} $$

for $p\in\mathbb{N}$ by [22, Theorem 2.3]. Another application of Proposition 5.6 yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\bigg[\mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\geq\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|+C\bigg\{\frac{R(X)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+\frac{R(X)^{2}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}\bigg\}\,p+\mbox{}\\
\qquad C\bigg\{\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)+R(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{E}\|X-\mathbf{E}X\|)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+\frac{R(X)(\mathbf{E}\|X-\mathbf{E}X\|^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}\bigg\}\sqrt{p}\bigg]\leq 2e^{-p} $$

for $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , provided the universal constant $C$ is chosen sufficiently large. Now recall that the matrix Bernstein inequality [77, eq. (6.1.4)] implies

$$ (\mathbf{E}\|X-\mathbf{E}X\|^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}\lesssim\sigma(X)\sqrt{\log d}+R(X)\log d\leq\sigma(X)\sqrt{p}+R(X)p $$

for $p\geq\log d$ . We can therefore further estimate

$$ \mathbf{P}\bigg[\mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\geq\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|+C\bigg\{\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)p+R(X)^{2}p^{\frac{3}{2}}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}+\mbox{}\\
\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{p}+R(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}p^{\frac{3}{4}}+R(X)p}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}\bigg\}\bigg]\leq 2e^{-p} $$

for $p\geq\log d$ , provided $C$ is chosen sufficiently large. The proof is now readily concluded by combining the above bounds and using $d^{\frac{1}{2p}}\leq e^{\frac{1}{2}}$ for $p\geq\log d$ . ∎

#### Remark 7.6.

We have emphasized in the introduction that the matrix Bernstein inequality may be viewed as a consequence of the universality principles of this paper. On the other hand, we have used the matrix Bernstein inequality in the proof of Lemma 7.5 to estimate the matrix norms that appear in Proposition 5.6. There is no circular reasoning here: the present section is only concerned with lower bounds on the spectrum of $X$ , while the matrix Bernstein inequality already follows from the upper bound of Proposition 7.4 (or from Theorem 2.9 by choosing $p\asymp\log d$ and $q=\infty$ ) and the noncommutative Khintchine inequality.

The same remark applies to the application of the matrix Bernstein inequality in the proof of Theorem 2.10 (cf. Lemma 6.12 in section 6.4).

We are now ready to prove the converse direction of Theorem 2.6.

#### Proposition 7.7.

For any $t\geq 0$ , we have

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{sp}(G)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(X)+C\varepsilon(t)[-1,1]\big]\geq 1-de^{-t}, $$

where $C$ is a universal constant and $\varepsilon(t)$ is as defined in Theorem 2.6.

#### Proof.

By following exactly the same steps as in the proof of Proposition 7.4, we can deduce using Lemmas 7.2 and Lemma 7.5 the inequality

$$ \mathbf{P}\bigg[\|(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}\|\leq C\bigg\{\|(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}\|+\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)t+R(X)^{2}t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\varepsilon^{3}}+\mbox{}\\
\frac{R(X)\sigma(X)^{2}t^{2}+R(X)^{3}t^{3}}{\varepsilon^{4}}+\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)t^{\frac{1}{2}}+R(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}t^{\frac{3}{4}}+R(X)t}{\varepsilon^{2}}\bigg\}\\
\mbox{for all }z\in\mathrm{sp}(G)+i\varepsilon\bigg]\geq 1-de^{-t} $$

for all $t,\varepsilon\geq 0$ , where $C$ is a universal constant. Thus Lemma 7.1 implies

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{sp}(G)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(X)+C\varepsilon^{\prime}(t)[-1,1]\big]\geq 1-de^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq 0$ and a universal constant $C$ , where

$$ \varepsilon^{\prime}(t)=\sigma_{*}(X)t^{\frac{1}{2}}+R(X)^{\frac{1}{3}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{2}{3}}t^{\frac{2}{3}}+R(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}t^{\frac{3}{4}}+R(X)t. $$

It remains to note that

$$ R(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}t^{\frac{3}{4}}\leq\frac{3}{4}R(X)^{\frac{1}{3}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{2}{3}}t^{\frac{2}{3}}+\frac{1}{4}R(X)t $$

by Young’s inequality, concluding the proof. ∎

We now conclude the proof of Theorem 2.6.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.6.

Combining Propositions 7.4 and 7.7 yields

$$ \mathbf{P}[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(G))>C\varepsilon(s)]\leq 2de^{-s} $$

for all $s\geq 0$ by the union bound. Choosing $s=2t$ , we obtain

$$ \mathbf{P}[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(G))>2C\varepsilon(t)]\leq 2de^{-2t}\leq de^{-t} $$

for $t\geq\log d$ , as the latter implies $2e^{-t}\leq\frac{2}{d}\leq 1$ by the standing assumption $d\geq 2$ . But for $t<\log d$ the inequality is trivial as then $de^{-t}>1$ . The tail bound follows.

To deduce the expectation bound, we note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{E}[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(G))] \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon(\log d)+\int_{C\varepsilon(\log d)}^{\infty}\mathbf{P}[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(G))>x]\,dx \displaystyle=C\varepsilon(\log d)+C\int_{\log d}^{\infty}\mathbf{P}[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(G))>C\varepsilon(t)]\,\frac{d\varepsilon(t)}{dt}\,dt \displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon(\log d)+2dC\int_{\log d}^{\infty}e^{-t}\,\frac{d\varepsilon(t)}{dt}\,dt\lesssim\varepsilon(\log d) $$

using $\int_{a}^{\infty}e^{-t}t^{\beta}\,dt\leq C_{\beta}e^{-a}a^{\beta}$ for $a>\frac{1}{4}$ , $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ , where $C_{\beta}$ depends only on $\beta$ . ∎

### 7.4. Proof of Corollary 2.7

Now that Theorem 2.6 has been established, the proof of Corollary 2.7 follows by routine manipulations.

#### Proof of Corollary 2.7.

We first note that

$$ \mathrm{sp}(A)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(B)+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon] $$

certainly implies

$$ \lambda_{\rm max}(A)\leq\lambda_{\rm max}(B)+\varepsilon $$

for any $A,B\in\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ . Thus

$$ |\lambda_{\rm max}(A)-\lambda_{\rm max}(B)|\leq\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(A),\mathrm{sp}(B)), $$

and the first and last bound of Corollary 2.7 follow immediately from Theorem 2.6.

To prove the middle bound, we note that a routine application of Gaussian concentration (see, e.g., [9, Corollary 4.14]) yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[|\lambda_{\rm max}(G)-\mathbf{E}\lambda_{\rm max}(G)|\geq\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{2t}\big]\leq 2e^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq 0$ . Combined with the first bound of Corollary 2.7, we obtain

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[|\lambda_{\rm max}(X)-\mathbf{E}\lambda_{\rm max}(G)|>\sigma_{*}(X)\sqrt{2t}+C\varepsilon(t)\big]\\
\leq 2e^{-t}+\mathbf{P}\big[|\lambda_{\rm max}(X)-\lambda_{\rm max}(G)|>C\varepsilon(t)\big]\leq(d+2)e^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq 0$ . The second inequality of Corollary 2.7 follows for a suitable choice of the universal constant (as in the last step of the proof of Theorem 2.6).

The analogous bounds for $\|X\|,\|G\|$ are proved in an identical manner. ∎

## 8. Truncation

The aim of this section is to prove Theorems 2.8 and 2.11. The basic idea behind these results is the following truncation argument. Let $X$ be as in (2.1), and let $G$ be the associated Gaussian model. Define the truncated model

$$ \tilde{X}:=Z_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}1_{\|Z_{i}\|\leq R}Z_{i}. $$

Then $X=\tilde{X}$ on the event $\{\max_{i}\|Z_{i}\|\leq R\}$ , while $R(\tilde{X})\leq R$ . We can therefore obtain universality principles for unbounded $X$ by conditioning on the above event, and applying the results of the previous sections to $\tilde{X}$ .

The problem with this approach is that it does not yield a comparison between the spectra of $X$ and $G$ , but rather between the spectra of $X$ and $\tilde{G}$ , where $\tilde{G}$ is the Gaussian model associated to $\tilde{X}$ . The main difficulty in the implementation of the truncation argument is therefore to compare the spectra of the Gaussian models $G$ and $\tilde{G}$ . To this end, we will first prove general comparison principles for the spectra of Gaussian random matrices in section 8.1. In section 8.2, we will upper bound the relevant parameters in the specific case of $G$ and $\tilde{G}$ . Finally, we combine these estimates in section 8.3 to complete the proof of Theorems 2.8 and 2.11.

### 8.1. Gaussian comparison principles

The aim of this section is to prove general comparison principles for the spectra of Gaussian random matrices. We begin by stating a comparison principle for the resolvent moments.

#### Lemma 8.1.

Let $H,\tilde{H}$ be self-adjoint Gaussian random matrices. Then we have

$$ \big|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H|^{-2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}-\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-\tilde{H}|^{-2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\big|\leq\frac{\|\mathbf{E}H-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}\|}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+2p\,\frac{\Delta(H,\tilde{H})}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}} $$

for any $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , where

$$ \Delta(H,\tilde{H}):=\sup_{\|M\|\leq 1}\big\|\mathbf{E}[(H-\mathbf{E}H)M(H-\mathbf{E}H)]-\mathbf{E}[(\tilde{H}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H})M(\tilde{H}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H})]\big\|. $$

#### Proof.

First, note that as $A^{-1}-B^{-1}=A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1}$ , we have

$$ \|(z\mathbf{1}-H)^{-1}-(z\mathbf{1}-(H-\mathbf{E}H+\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}))^{-1}\|\leq\frac{\|\mathbf{E}H-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}\|}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}. $$

Thus we can assume in the sequel that $\mathbf{E}H=\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}$ .

Assume without loss of generality that $H,\tilde{H}$ are independent and $\mathbf{E}H=\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}$ , and let $Y,\tilde{Y}$ be independent copies of $H-\mathbf{E}H$ and $\tilde{H}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}$ , respectively. Define

$$ H(t):=\mathbf{E}H+\sqrt{t}\,(H-\mathbf{E}H)+\sqrt{1-t}\,(\tilde{H}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}). $$

By the Gaussian interpolation lemma [9, Lemma 4.11]

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H(t)|^{-2p}]=\frac{\mathbf{E}[\partial_{Y}^{2}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H(t)|^{-2p}]-\mathbf{E}[\partial_{\tilde{Y}}^{2}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H(t)|^{-2p}]}{2}. $$

By the product rule, we have

$$ \partial_{B}^{2}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H|^{-2p}=2p\sum_{k=0}^{p}\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[B(z\mathbf{1}-H)^{-k-1}B(z\mathbf{1}-H)^{-p-1+k}(\bar{z}\mathbf{1}-H)^{-p}]\\
+2p\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[B(z\mathbf{1}-H)^{-p-1}(\bar{z}\mathbf{1}-H)^{-k-1}B(\bar{z}\mathbf{1}-H)^{-p+k}]. $$

We can therefore bound

$$ \bigg|\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H(t)|^{-2p}]\bigg|\leq p(2p+1)\,\Delta(H,\tilde{H})\,\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H(t)|^{-2p-2}] $$

by applying Lemma 5.2 to $F(M,M^{\prime}):=\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}YMYM^{\prime}]-\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\tilde{Y}M\tilde{Y}M^{\prime}]$ as in the proof of Lemma 5.3, and using $\sup_{\|M\|\leq 1,\|M^{\prime}\|_{1}\leq 1}|F(M,M^{\prime})|=\Delta(H,\tilde{H})$ .

It remains to note that $\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H(t)|^{-2p-2}]\leq(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{-3}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H(t)|^{-2p}]^{1-\frac{1}{2p}}$ and the chain rule readily yield the estimate

$$ \bigg|\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H(t)|^{-2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\bigg|\leq(p+\tfrac{1}{2})\,\frac{\Delta(H,\tilde{H})}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}. $$

The conclusion now follows by integrating over $t$ (using $p+\frac{1}{2}\leq 2p$ ). ∎

A bound on the Hausdorff distance now follows along familiar lines.

#### Proposition 8.2.

Let $H,\tilde{H}$ be self-adjoint Gaussian random matrices. Then

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(H),\mathrm{sp}(\tilde{H}))>C\{\|\mathbf{E}H-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}\|+\Delta(H,\tilde{H})^{\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{\log d}\\
+(\sigma_{*}(H)+\sigma_{*}(\tilde{H}))x\}\big]\leq de^{-x^{2}} $$

for all $x\geq 0$ , where $C$ is a universal constant and $\Delta(H,\tilde{H})$ is as in Lemma 8.1.

#### Proof.

Note first that

$$ \mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-H|^{-2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\leq\mathbf{E}[\|(z\mathbf{1}-H)^{-1}\|^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\leq\mathbf{E}\|(z\mathbf{1}-H)^{-1}\|+C\sqrt{p}\frac{\sigma_{*}(H)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}} $$

for a universal constant $C$ as in the proof of Lemma 7.3. On the other hand,

$$ \mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|z\mathbf{1}-\tilde{H}|^{-2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\geq d^{-\frac{1}{2p}}\mathbf{E}\|(z\mathbf{1}-\tilde{H})^{-1}\|. $$

Combining these bounds with Lemmas 5.5 and 8.1 yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\bigg[d^{-\frac{1}{2p}}\|(z\mathbf{1}-\tilde{H})^{-1}\|\geq\|(z\mathbf{1}-H)^{-1}\|+\frac{\|\mathbf{E}H-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}\|}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+2p\,\frac{\Delta(H,\tilde{H})}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}\\
+C\sqrt{p}\frac{\sigma_{*}(H)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+\frac{\sigma_{*}(\tilde{H})+\sigma_{*}(H)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}\,x\bigg]\leq 4e^{-x^{2}/2}. $$

Choosing $p=\lfloor\log d\rfloor$ and proceeding as in the proof of Proposition 7.4 yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\bigg[\|(z\mathbf{1}-\tilde{H})^{-1}\|\geq L\bigg\{\|(z\mathbf{1}-H)^{-1}\|+\frac{\|\mathbf{E}H-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}\|}{\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{\Delta(H,\tilde{H})\log d}{\varepsilon^{3}}\\
+\frac{\sigma_{*}(\tilde{H})+\sigma_{*}(H)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\,x\bigg\}\text{ for some }z\in\mathrm{sp}(\tilde{H})+i\varepsilon\bigg]\leq de^{-x^{2}} $$

for all $x\geq 0$ , where $L$ is a universal constant. The same bound holds if we reverse the roles of $H$ and $\tilde{H}$ , and the conclusion follows readily from Lemma 7.1. ∎

We finally formulate a variant of Lemma 8.1 for the resolvent.

#### Lemma 8.3.

Let $H,\tilde{H}$ be self-adjoint Gaussian random matrices. Then we have

$$ \big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-H)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-\tilde{H})^{-1}]\big\|\leq\frac{\|\mathbf{E}H-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}\|}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+\frac{\Delta(H,\tilde{H})}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}, $$

where $\Delta(H,\tilde{H})$ is as in Lemma 8.1.

#### Proof.

As in the proof of Lemma 8.1, it suffices to assume that $\mathbf{E}H=\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}$ . Moreover, applying Gaussian interpolation as in the proof of Lemma 8.1 yields

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E}[\langle v,(z\mathbf{1}-H(t))^{-1}w\rangle]=\mathbf{E}[\langle v,(z\mathbf{1}-H(t))^{-1}Y(z\mathbf{1}-H(t))^{-1}Y(z\mathbf{1}-H(t))^{-1}w\rangle]\\
-\mathbf{E}[\langle v,(z\mathbf{1}-H(t))^{-1}\tilde{Y}(z\mathbf{1}-H(t))^{-1}\tilde{Y}(z\mathbf{1}-H(t))^{-1}w\rangle]. $$

Integrating this identity and taking the supremum over $v,w$ with $\|v\|=\|w\|=1$ readily yields the conclusion, where we use that $Y,\tilde{Y}$ are independent of $H(t)$ . ∎

### 8.2. The truncation error

In order to apply the above comparison principles to $G,\tilde{G}$ , we must estimate the relevant parameters in this case.

#### Lemma 8.4.

$\|\mathbf{E}G-\mathbf{E}\tilde{G}\|\leq\sqrt{2}\,\sigma_{*}(X)$ for $R\geq\sqrt{2}\,\bar{R}(X)$ .

#### Proof.

We first note that as $\mathbf{E}X=Z_{0}$ and by the independence of $Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n}$

$$ \mathbf{E}\tilde{G}-\mathbf{E}G=\mathbf{E}\tilde{X}-\mathbf{E}X=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[1_{\|Z_{i}\|\leq R}Z_{i}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}^{-1}\mathbf{E}[1_{\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|\leq R}Z_{i}], $$

where $b_{i}:=\mathbf{P}[\max_{j\neq i}\|Z_{j}\|\leq R]\geq\mathbf{P}[\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|\leq R]$ . We therefore obtain

$$ \|\mathbf{E}\tilde{G}-\mathbf{E}G\|=\sup_{\|v\|=\|w\|=1}\bigg|\mathbf{E}\bigg[1_{\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|\leq R}\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}^{-1}\langle v,Z_{i}w\rangle\bigg]\bigg|\leq\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)}{\mathbf{P}[\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|\leq R]^{\frac{1}{2}}} $$

by Cauchy-Schwarz. It remains to note that $\mathbf{P}[\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|\leq R]\geq\frac{1}{2}$ whenever $R\geq\sqrt{2}\,\mathbf{E}[\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|^{2}]^{\frac{1}{2}}=:\sqrt{2}\,\bar{R}(X)$ by Markov’s inequality. ∎

#### Lemma 8.5.

$\Delta(G,\tilde{G})\leq 24\,\bar{R}(X)\sigma(X)$ for $R\geq\bar{R}(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose first that $M\geq 0$ with $\|M\|\leq 1$ . We begin by writing

$$ \mathbf{E}[(G-\mathbf{E}G)M(G-\mathbf{E}G)]-\mathbf{E}[(\tilde{G}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{G})M(\tilde{G}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{G})]=\\
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big\{\mathbf{E}[1_{\|Z_{i}\|>R}Z_{i}MZ_{i}]+\mathbf{E}[1_{\|Z_{i}\|\leq R}Z_{i}]\,M\,\mathbf{E}[1_{\|Z_{i}\|\leq R}Z_{i}]\big\}\geq 0. $$

Now note that as $\mathbf{E}[Z_{i}]=0$ , we have $\mathbf{E}[1_{\|Z_{i}\|\leq R}Z_{i}]=-\mathbf{E}[1_{\|Z_{i}\|>R}Z_{i}]$ . Moreover, for any self-adjoint random matrix $Y$ , we have $\mathbf{E}[Y]\,M\,\mathbf{E}[Y]\leq\mathbf{E}[Y]^{2}\leq\mathbf{E}[Y^{2}]$ using $\|M\|\leq 1$ and Jensen’s inequality. We therefore obtain

$$ \|\mathbf{E}[(G-\mathbf{E}G)M(G-\mathbf{E}G)]-\mathbf{E}[(\tilde{G}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{G})M(\tilde{G}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{G})]\|\leq 2\!\sup_{\|v\|=1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[1_{\|Z_{i}\|>R}\|Z_{i}v\|^{2}]. $$

To proceed, let $Z_{i}^{\prime}$ be independent copies of $Z_{i}$ , and note that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[1_{\|Z_{i}\|>R}\|Z_{i}v\|^{2}]\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[1_{\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|>R}\|Z_{i}v\|^{2}] \displaystyle\qquad\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[1_{\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|>R}(\|Z_{i}v\|^{2}-\|Z_{i}^{\prime}v\|^{2})]+\mathbf{P}[{\textstyle\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|>R}]\,\sigma(X)^{2} $$

for $\|v\|=1$ . Moreover, we have

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[1_{\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|>R}(\|Z_{i}v\|^{2}-\|Z_{i}^{\prime}v\|^{2})]\leq\mathbf{E}\bigg[\bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\|Z_{i}v\|^{2}-\|Z_{i}^{\prime}v\|^{2})\bigg|\bigg]=\\
\mathbf{E}\bigg[\bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varepsilon_{i}(\|Z_{i}v\|^{2}-\|Z_{i}^{\prime}v\|^{2})\bigg|\bigg]\leq 2\,\mathbf{E}\bigg[\bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varepsilon_{i}\|Z_{i}v\|^{2}\bigg|\bigg]\leq 2\,\mathbf{E}\bigg[\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|Z_{i}v\|^{4}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigg], $$

where $\varepsilon_{i}$ are i.i.d. random signs that are independent of the other variables, we used that the distribution of $(Z_{i},Z_{i}^{\prime})$ is invariant under exchanging $Z_{i}$ and $Z_{i}^{\prime}$ for any $i$ , and we applied Jensen’s inequality conditionally on $(Z_{i})$ in the last inequality. Bounding $\|Z_{i}v\|^{4}\leq(\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|^{2})\|Z_{i}v\|^{2}$ and applying Cauchy-Schwarz yields

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[1_{\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|>R}(\|Z_{i}v\|^{2}-\|Z_{i}^{\prime}v\|^{2})]\leq 2\,\mathbf{E}[{\textstyle\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|^{2}}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X) $$

for $\|v\|=1$ . Putting together all the above estimates yields

$$ \|\mathbf{E}[(G-\mathbf{E}G)M(G-\mathbf{E}G)]-\mathbf{E}[(\tilde{G}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{G})M(\tilde{G}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{G})]\|\leq\\
2\,\mathbf{P}[{\textstyle\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|>R}]\,\sigma(X)^{2}+4\,\mathbf{E}[{\textstyle\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|^{2}}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X)\leq 6\,\mathbf{E}[{\textstyle\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|^{2}}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X) $$

for $R\geq\mathbf{E}[{\textstyle\max_{j}\|Z_{j}\|^{2}}]^{\frac{1}{4}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ using Markov’s inequality in the last step.

Finally, note that any matrix $M$ with $\|M\|\leq 1$ can be written as $M=\mathrm{Re}\,M+i\,\mathrm{Im}\,M$ with $\|\mathrm{Re}\,M\|=\frac{1}{2}\|M+M^{*}\|\leq 1$ and $\|\mathrm{Im}\,M\|=\frac{1}{2}\|M-M^{*}\|\leq 1$ . As any self-adjoint matrix is the difference of its positive and negative parts, we can write $M=M_{1}-M_{2}+iM_{3}-iM_{4}$ with $M_{i}\geq 0$ with $\|M_{i}\|\leq 1$ . Applying the above estimate to each $M_{i}$ and using the triangle inequality concludes the proof. ∎

Finally, we must bound the matrix parameters of $\tilde{X}$ .

#### Lemma 8.6.

We have $R(\tilde{X})\leq 2R$ , $\sigma_{*}(\tilde{X})\leq\sigma_{*}(X)$ , and $\sigma(\tilde{X})\leq\sigma(X)$ .

#### Proof.

The first inequality follows immediately from

$$ R(\tilde{X})=\Big\|\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\big\|1_{\|Z_{i}\|\leq R}Z_{i}-\mathbf{E}[1_{\|Z_{i}\|\leq R}Z_{i}]\big\|\Big\|_{\infty} $$

and the triangle inequality. Next, note that for any (complex) random variable $Y$ and event $A$ , we have $\mathbf{E}[|1_{A}Y-\mathbf{E}[1_{A}Y]|^{2}]\leq\mathbf{E}[1_{A}|Y|^{2}]\leq\mathbf{E}[|Y|^{2}]$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{E}[|\langle v,(\tilde{X}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{X})w\rangle|^{2}] \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[|1_{\|Z_{i}\|\leq R}\langle v,Z_{i}w\rangle-\mathbf{E}[1_{\|Z_{i}\|\leq R}\langle v,Z_{i}w\rangle]|^{2}] \displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[|\langle v,Z_{i}w\rangle|^{2}]=\mathbf{E}[|\langle v,(X-\mathbf{E}X)w\rangle|^{2}] $$

for any nonrandom vectors $v,w$ . The remaining bounds follow, respectively, by taking the supremum over $\|v\|=\|w\|=1$ , or by summing over the coordinate basis $w=e_{k}$ and then taking the supremum over $\|v\|=1$ . ∎

### 8.3. Proof of Theorems 2.8 and 2.11

We now put everything together.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.8.

As $X=\tilde{X}$ on the event $\{\max_{i}\|Z_{i}\|\leq R\}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{P}\Big[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(\tilde{G}))>C\tilde{\varepsilon}(t),~\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|Z_{i}\|\leq R\Big] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\leq\mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(\tilde{X}),\mathrm{sp}(\tilde{G}))>C\tilde{\varepsilon}(t)\big]\leq de^{-t} $$

with

$$ \tilde{\varepsilon}(t):=\sigma_{*}(\tilde{X})\,t^{\frac{1}{2}}+R(\tilde{X})^{\frac{1}{3}}\sigma(\tilde{X})^{\frac{2}{3}}t^{\frac{2}{3}}+R(\tilde{X})\,t. $$

from Theorem 2.6. Moreover, we can replace $\tilde{\varepsilon}(t)$ by $\varepsilon_{R}(t)$ on the left-hand side of the above inequality as $\tilde{\varepsilon}(t)\leq\varepsilon_{R}(t)$ by Lemma 8.6.

On the other hand, Proposition 8.2 and Lemmas 8.4, 8.5 and 8.6 imply

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(\tilde{G}),\mathrm{sp}(G))>C\{R+\sigma_{*}(X)\}t^{\frac{1}{2}}\big]\leq de^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq 0$ and $R\geq R_{0}:=\bar{R}(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}+\sqrt{2}\,\bar{R}(X)$ . Here we used that we may assume without loss of generality that $t\geq\log d$ in the above estimate (as otherwise the right-hand side exceeds one and the bound is trivial), and that $\Delta(G,\tilde{G})\leq 24R^{2}$ by the assumption on $R$ and Lemma 8.5. We may once again replace $\{R+\sigma_{*}(X)\}t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ by $\varepsilon_{R}(t)$ on the left-hand side as $t^{\frac{1}{2}}\lesssim t$ for $t\geq\log d$ .

Combining the above bounds, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{P}\Big[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(G))>2C\varepsilon_{R}(t),~\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|Z_{i}\|\leq R\Big] \displaystyle\leq\mathbf{P}\Big[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(\tilde{G}))+\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(\tilde{G}),\mathrm{sp}(G))>2C\varepsilon_{R}(t),~\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|Z_{i}\|\leq R\Big] \displaystyle\leq\mathbf{P}\Big[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(\tilde{G}))>C\varepsilon_{R}(t),~\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|Z_{i}\|\leq R\Big] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(\tilde{G}),\mathrm{sp}(G))>C\varepsilon_{R}(t)\big]\leq 2de^{-t}. $$

As in the proof of Theorem 2.6, the upper bound can be replaced by $de^{-t}$ if we increase the value of the universal constant on the left-hand side.

This concludes the proof of the tail bound. To prove the expectation bound, note that choosing $R=R_{0}t$ in the tail bound yields

$$ \mathbf{P}[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(G))>C\delta(t)]\leq e^{-t/2}+\mathbf{P}\bigg[\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|Z_{i}\|>R_{0}t\bigg] $$

for $t\geq 2\log d$ , where

$$ \delta(t):=\sigma_{*}(X)\,t^{\frac{1}{2}}+R_{0}^{\frac{1}{3}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{2}{3}}t+R_{0}t^{2} $$

and we used $de^{-t}\leq e^{-t/2}$ for $t\geq 2\log d$ . We now compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{E}[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(G))]\leq C\delta(2\log d)+\int_{C\delta(2\log 2)}^{\infty}\mathbf{P}[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(G))>x]\,dx \displaystyle=C\delta(2\log d)+C\int_{2\log d}^{\infty}\mathbf{P}[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(G))>C\delta(t)]\,\frac{d\delta(t)}{dt}\,dt \displaystyle\leq C\delta(2\log d)+C\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t/2}\frac{d\delta(t)}{dt}\,dt+C\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbf{P}\bigg[\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|Z_{i}\|>R_{0}t\bigg]\,\frac{d\delta(t)}{dt}\,dt \displaystyle\lesssim\delta(2\log d)+\mathbf{E}[\delta({\textstyle\max_{i}\|Z_{i}\|/R_{0}})]\lesssim\delta(2\log d).\phantom{\int} $$

The conclusion follows readily using the assumption $\bar{R}(X)\,(\log d)^{3}\lesssim\sigma(X)$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 2.11.

As $X=\tilde{X}$ on the event $\{\max_{i}\|Z_{i}\|\leq R\}$ , we have

$$ \mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]=\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-\tilde{X})^{-1}]+\mathbf{E}[\{(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}-(z\mathbf{1}-\tilde{X})^{-1}\}1_{\max_{i}\|Z_{i}\|>R}]. $$

Thus Markov’s inequality yields

$$ \big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-\tilde{X})^{-1}]\big\|\leq\frac{2\,\mathbf{P}[\max_{i}\|Z_{i}\|>R]}{\mathrm{Im}\,z}\leq\frac{2\bar{R}(X)^{2}}{R^{2}\,\mathrm{Im}\,z}. $$

Applying Theorem 2.10 and Lemmas 8.3, 8.4, 8.5 and 8.6 yields

$$ \big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}]\big\|\lesssim\frac{\bar{R}(X)^{2}}{R^{2}\,\mathrm{Im}\,z}+\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+\frac{R^{2}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{3}}+\frac{R\sigma(X)^{2}+R^{3}\log d}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{4}} $$

for $R\geq R_{0}:=\bar{R}(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}+\sqrt{2}\,\bar{R}(X)$ .

Now assume first that $\mathrm{Im}\,z\geq R_{0}$ and choose $R=R_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ . Then we obtain

$$ \big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}]\big\|\lesssim\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)+R_{0}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}+\frac{R_{0}^{\frac{3}{2}}\log d}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{\frac{5}{2}}}+\frac{R_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(X)^{2}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{\frac{7}{2}}}. $$

In particular, if $\mathrm{Im}\,z\geq R_{0}^{\frac{1}{5}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{4}{5}}+R_{0}(\log d)^{\frac{2}{3}}$ , we obtain

$$ \big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}]\big\|\lesssim\frac{\sigma_{*}(X)+R_{0}^{\frac{1}{5}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{4}{5}}+R_{0}(\log d)^{\frac{2}{3}}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}. $$

On the other hand, for $\mathrm{Im}\,z<R_{0}^{\frac{1}{5}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{4}{5}}+R_{0}(\log d)^{\frac{2}{3}}$ we can estimate

$$ \big\|\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-X)^{-1}]-\mathbf{E}[(z\mathbf{1}-G)^{-1}]\big\|\leq\frac{2}{\mathrm{Im}\,z}\lesssim\frac{R_{0}^{\frac{1}{5}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{4}{5}}+R_{0}(\log d)^{\frac{2}{3}}}{(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^{2}}. $$

If $\bar{R}(X)(\log d)^{\frac{5}{3}}\lesssim\sigma(X)$ , then $R_{0}(\log d)^{\frac{2}{3}}\lesssim R_{0}^{\frac{1}{5}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{4}{5}}\asymp\bar{R}(X)^{\frac{1}{10}}\sigma(X)^{\frac{9}{10}}$ , and the first part of the theorem follows. The second part of the theorem now follows from [9, Lemma 5.11] as in the proof of Theorem 2.10. ∎

## 9. Applications: Proofs

### 9.1. Random lifts

The aim of this section is to prove Theorem 3.13. We will first prove a more general result, and then specialize to the case of lifts.

#### 9.1.1. Strong convergence

In this section, we let $\Pi_{1},\ldots,\Pi_{k}$ be i.i.d. uniformly distributed random $n\times n$ permutation matrices, and we fix $A_{1},\ldots,A_{k}\in\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})$ . We consider the random matrix

$$ X=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}\otimes\Pi_{i}+A_{i}^{*}\otimes\Pi_{i}^{*}), $$

and let $X^{\perp}$ be its restriction to $\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes 1^{\perp}$ . Recall that if $s_{1},\ldots,s_{2k}$ is a free semicircular family, then $c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}$ defined by $c_{j}=\frac{s_{j}+is_{k+j}}{\sqrt{2}}$ is a free circular family.

#### Proposition 9.1.

Let $c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}$ be a free circular family, and define

$$ X_{\mathrm{F}}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\big\{\big((1-\varepsilon^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}A_{i}+\varepsilon A_{i}^{*}\big)\otimes c_{i}+\big((1-\varepsilon^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}A_{i}+\varepsilon A_{i}^{*}\big)^{*}\otimes c_{i}^{*}\big\} $$

with $\varepsilon=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}(\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{n-2})}$ . Then

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\|X^{\perp}\|\geq\|X_{\rm F}\|+C\big\{v^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}(\log nd)^{\frac{3}{4}}+vt^{\frac{1}{2}}+R^{\frac{1}{3}}\sigma^{\frac{2}{3}}t^{\frac{2}{3}}+Rt\big\}\big]\leq 2nde^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq 0$ , where $C$ is a universal constant and

$$ \sigma=\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}\bigg(A_{i}A_{i}^{*}+A_{i}^{*}A_{i}+\frac{A_{i}^{2}+A_{i}^{*2}}{n-1}\bigg)\bigg\|^{\frac{1}{2}},\qquad R=2\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\|A_{i}\|, $$

and

$$ v=\frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}}\,\bigg\|\mathrm{Cov}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{k}A_{i}g_{i}\bigg)\bigg\|^{\frac{1}{2}}, $$

where $g_{1},\ldots,g_{k}$ are i.i.d. standard real Gaussians.

Proposition 9.1 is an immediate consequence of Theorem 2.16 once we prove that $\sigma(X^{\perp})=\sigma$ , $R(X^{\perp})\leq R$ , $\sigma_{*}(X^{\perp})\leq v(X^{\perp})\leq v$ , and $\|X^{\perp}_{\rm free}\|=\|X_{\rm F}\|$ . These facts will be established in the following lemmas, concluding the proof.

#### Lemma 9.2.

We have $\sigma(X^{\perp})=\sigma$ and $R(X^{\perp})\leq R$ .

#### Proof.

The bound on $R(X^{\perp})$ follows immediately from $\|\Pi_{i}\|=1$ . To compute $\sigma(X^{\perp})$ , we note that the restriction of $\Pi_{i}$ to $1^{\perp}$ a random matrix as in Lemma 3.5 with $d=n-1$ and $s=1$ (as this is an $(n-1)$ -dimensional real representation of the symmetric group; alternatively, the conclusions of Lemma 3.5 can be verified in this case by a direct computation). We can therefore compute

$$ \mathbf{E}[X^{\perp}]=0,\qquad\mathbf{E}[(X^{\perp})^{2}]=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\bigg(A_{i}A_{i}^{*}+A_{i}^{*}A_{i}+\frac{A_{i}^{2}+A_{i}^{*2}}{n-1}\bigg)\otimes\mathbf{1}, $$

and the conclusion follows immediately. ∎

#### Lemma 9.3.

We have $\|X_{\rm free}^{\perp}\|=\|X_{\mathrm{F}}\|$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\bar{c}_{i}:=(1-\varepsilon^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}c_{i}+\varepsilon c_{i}^{*}$ . Then we write

$$ X_{\rm free}^{\perp}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}\otimes\Pi_{i,\mathrm{free}}^{\perp}+A_{i}^{*}\otimes\bar{\Pi}_{i,\mathrm{free}}^{\perp*}),\qquad X_{\rm F}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}\otimes\bar{c}_{i}+A_{i}^{*}\otimes\bar{c}_{i}^{*}). $$

Now note that

$$ \tau(\bar{c}_{i})=0,\qquad\tau(\bar{c}_{i}\bar{c}_{i}^{*})=\tau(\bar{c}_{i}^{*}\bar{c}_{i})=1,\qquad\tau(\bar{c}_{i}^{2})=\tau((\bar{c}_{i}^{*})^{2})=\frac{1}{n-1}, $$

while applying Lemma 3.5 as in the proof of Lemma 9.2 yields

$$ \mathbf{E}[\Pi_{i}^{\perp}]=0,\quad\mathbf{E}[\Pi_{i}^{\perp}\Pi_{i}^{\perp*}]=\mathbf{E}[\Pi_{i}^{\perp*}\Pi_{i}^{\perp}]=\mathbf{1},\quad\mathbf{E}[(\Pi_{i}^{\perp})^{2}]=\mathbf{E}[(\Pi_{i}^{\perp*})^{2}]=\frac{1}{n-1}\mathbf{1}. $$

The conclusion follows as in the proof of [9, Lemma 7.9]. ∎

#### Lemma 9.4.

We have $v(X^{\perp})\leq v$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 3.5, we have

$$ \mathrm{Cov}(A_{i}\otimes\Pi_{i}^{\perp})=\iota(A_{i})\iota(A_{i})^{*}\otimes\mathrm{Cov}(\Pi_{i}^{\perp})=\iota(A_{i})\iota(A_{i})^{*}\otimes\frac{1}{n-1}\mathbf{1}, $$

where $\iota:\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{C}^{d^{2}}$ maps a matrix to its vector of entries. Therefore, as $\Pi_{1},\ldots,\Pi_{k}$ are independent, we have

$$ \mathrm{Cov}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{k}A_{i}\otimes\Pi_{i}^{\perp}\bigg)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathrm{Cov}(A_{i}\otimes\Pi_{i}^{\perp})=\frac{1}{n-1}\mathrm{Cov}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{k}A_{i}g_{i}\bigg)\otimes\mathbf{1}. $$

The conclusion follows from the triangle inequality $v(A+B)\leq v(A)+v(B)$ . ∎

#### 9.1.2. Free generators and circular variables

The operator $X_{\rm F}$ in Proposition 9.1 is defined by a free circular family. In the study of random lifts, however, we are interested in the analogous operator where the circular variables $c_{i}$ are replaced by the left-regular representation $\lambda(g_{i})$ of the free generators of $\mathrm{F}_{k}$ . We presently establish a comparison principle between these objects.

#### Proposition 9.5.

Let $c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}$ be a free circular family and let $g_{1},\ldots,g_{k}$ be free generators of $\mathrm{F}_{k}$ . Then for any $A_{1},\ldots,A_{k}\in\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})$ , we have

$$ \bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}\otimes c_{i}+A_{i}^{*}\otimes c_{i}^{*})\bigg\|\leq\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}\otimes\lambda(g_{i})+A_{i}^{*}\otimes\lambda(g_{i})^{*})\bigg\|+2\tilde{\sigma}^{\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{R}^{\frac{1}{2}}, $$

where $\tilde{\sigma}^{2}=\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}A_{i}^{*}+A_{i}^{*}A_{i})\|$ and $\tilde{R}=\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\|A_{i}\|$ .

#### Proof.

We proceed in several steps.

Step 1. We begin by noting that if $c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}$ is a circular family, $c_{1}^{*},\ldots,c_{k}^{*}$ is also a circular family. We can therefore write

$$ \bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}\otimes c_{i}+A_{i}^{*}\otimes c_{i}^{*})\bigg\|=\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}^{*}\otimes c_{i}+A_{i}\otimes c_{i}^{*})\bigg\|=\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\tilde{A}_{i}\otimes c_{i}+\tilde{B}_{i}\otimes c_{i}^{*})\bigg\|, $$

where we defined the self-adjoint matrices

$$ \tilde{A}_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}0&A_{i}\\
A_{i}^{*}&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad\quad\tilde{B}_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}0&A_{i}^{*}\\
A_{i}&0\end{bmatrix}. $$

Similarly, if $g_{1},\ldots,g_{k}$ are free generators of $\mathrm{F}_{k}$ , then $g_{1}^{-1},\ldots,g_{k}^{-1}$ are as well, and thus the analogous identities holds when $c_{i}$ is replaced by $\lambda(g_{i})$ .

Step 2. For any $A,M\in\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}$ with $M>0$ , define

$$ \mathrm{R}_{A}(M)=M^{\frac{1}{2}}\big(\big(\mathbf{1}+(M^{-\frac{1}{2}}AM^{-\frac{1}{2}})^{2}\big)^{\frac{1}{2}}-\mathbf{1}\big)M^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Then by [54, Theorem 1.1 and p. 454], we have

$$ \bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\tilde{A}_{i}\otimes\lambda(g_{i})+\tilde{B}_{i}\otimes\lambda(g_{i})^{*})\bigg\|=\inf_{M>0}\bigg\|2M+\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\mathrm{R}_{\tilde{A}_{i}}(M)+\mathrm{R}_{\tilde{B}_{i}}(M))\bigg\|. $$

On the other hand, as the circular family $c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}$ can be realized by setting $c_{i}=l_{i}+l_{k+i}^{*}$ where $l_{1},\ldots,l_{2k}$ are canoncial creation operators on the free Fock space (cf. [54, §1.2]), we obtain by [54, Corollary 1.4]

$$ \bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\tilde{A}_{i}\otimes c_{i}+\tilde{B}_{i}\otimes c_{i}^{*})\bigg\|\leq\inf_{M>0}\bigg\|2M+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\tilde{A}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{A}_{i}+\tilde{B}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{B}_{i}}{2}\bigg\|. $$

Step 3. We claim that for any $\delta>0$ , there exists $M\geq\frac{\delta}{2}\mathbf{1}$ so that

$$ 2M+\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\mathrm{R}_{\tilde{A}_{i}}(M)+\mathrm{R}_{\tilde{B}_{i}}(M))=\bigg(\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\tilde{A}_{i}\otimes\lambda(g_{i})+\tilde{B}_{i}\otimes\lambda(g_{i})^{*})\bigg\|+\delta\bigg)\mathbf{1}. $$

Indeed, let $\tilde{g}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{2k}$ be the free generators of the free product $\mathbb{Z}_{2}*\cdots*\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ of $2k$ copies of $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ , and define the operator $\tilde{X}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\tilde{A}_{i}\otimes\lambda(\tilde{g}_{i})+\tilde{B}_{i}\otimes\lambda(\tilde{g}_{i+k}))$ . Then [54, Theorem 1.1, Lemma 2.3 and Proposition 3.1] show that the above identity is satisfied if we choose the matrix $M$ so that $(2M)^{-1}=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\tau)\big[\big((\|\tilde{X}\|+\delta)\mathbf{1}-\tilde{X}\big)^{-1}\big]$ . As $\|\tilde{X}\|\mathbf{1}-\tilde{X}\geq 0$ , we clearly have $(2M)^{-1}\leq\delta^{-1}\mathbf{1}$ , establishing the claim.

Step 4. Define the function

$$ h(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{2}-((1+x^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}-1)=\frac{x^{4}}{2((1+x^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}+1)^{2}}. $$

Then clearly $h(x)\leq\frac{1}{8}x^{4}$ . Thus we have for any self-adjoint $A,M$ with $M>0$

$$ \frac{AM^{-1}A}{2}\leq\mathrm{R}_{A}(M)+\frac{AM^{-1}AM^{-1}AM^{-1}A}{8}, $$

where we used that $\frac{1}{2}AM^{-1}A-\mathrm{R}_{A}(M)=M^{\frac{1}{2}}h(M^{-\frac{1}{2}}AM^{-\frac{1}{2}})M^{\frac{1}{2}}$ .

Step 5. We now put everything together. Let $\delta>0$ and choose $M$ as in Step 3. Then we can estimate

$$ \displaystyle\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}\otimes c_{i}+A_{i}^{*}\otimes c_{i}^{*})\bigg\|\leq\bigg\|2M+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\tilde{A}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{A}_{i}+\tilde{B}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{B}_{i}}{2}\bigg\| \displaystyle\leq\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}\otimes\lambda(g_{i})+A_{i}^{*}\otimes\lambda(g_{i})^{*})\bigg\|+\delta \displaystyle\qquad\quad+\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\tilde{A}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{A}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{A}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{A}_{i}+\tilde{B}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{B}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{B}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{B}_{i}}{8}\bigg\| \displaystyle\leq\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{i}\otimes\lambda(g_{i})+A_{i}^{*}\otimes\lambda(g_{i})^{*})\bigg\|+\delta+\frac{\max_{i}(\|\tilde{A}_{i}\|^{2}\vee\|\tilde{B}_{i}\|^{2})}{\delta^{3}}\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\tilde{A}_{i}^{2}+\tilde{B}_{i}^{2})\bigg\|, $$

where we used $\langle v,\tilde{A}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{A}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{A}_{i}M^{-1}\tilde{A}_{i}v\rangle\leq\|\tilde{A}_{i}v\|^{2}\|M^{-1}\|^{3}\|\tilde{A}_{i}\|^{2}$ (and analogously for $\tilde{B}_{i}$ ) and $M\geq\frac{\delta}{2}$ in the last line. As $\max_{i}(\|\tilde{A}_{i}\|^{2}\vee\|\tilde{B}_{i}\|^{2})=\tilde{R}^{2}$ and $\|\sum_{i}(\tilde{A}_{i}^{2}+\tilde{B}_{i}^{2})\|=\tilde{\sigma}^{2}$ , the conclusion follows by choosing $\delta=\tilde{\sigma}^{\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{R}^{\frac{1}{2}}$ . ∎

#### 9.1.3. Random $n$ -lifts

We now specialize the above results to the situation of random $n$ -lifts. That is, we fix a base graph $H=([d],E_{H})$ , set $k=|E_{H}|$ , and $A_{e}=e_{i}e_{j}^{*}$ for $e=(i,j)\in E_{H}$ , $i\leq j$ . Then the random matrix $X=X^{(n)}$ is the adjacency matrix of the random $n$ -lift of $H$ . Let us begin by estimating the parameters that appear in Propositions 9.1 and 9.5 in this case.

#### Lemma 9.6.

Denote by $\mathrm{D}(H)$ the maximal degree of a vertex of $H$ and by $\mathrm{M}(H)$ the maximal multiplicity of an edge of $H$ . Then we have

$$ \tilde{\sigma}^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}\leq 2\,\mathrm{D}(H),\qquad v^{2}=\frac{4\,\mathrm{M}(H)}{n-1},\qquad\tilde{R}\leq R\leq 2. $$

#### Proof.

That $\tilde{R}\leq R\leq 2$ is immediate. Now let $A_{e}=e_{i}e_{j}^{*}$ for $e=(i,j)\in E_{H}$ . Then $A_{e}A_{e}^{*}+A_{e}^{*}A_{e}=e_{i}e_{i}^{*}+e_{j}e_{j}^{*}$ and $A_{e}^{2}+A_{e}^{*2}=2e_{i}e_{i}^{*}1_{i=j}$ . Therefore

$$ \bigg\|\sum_{e\in E_{H}}(A_{e}A_{e}^{*}+A_{e}^{*}A_{e})\bigg\|=\mathrm{D}(H),\qquad\bigg\|\sum_{e\in E_{H}}(A_{e}^{2}+A_{e}^{*2})\bigg\|=2\,\mathrm{L}(H)\leq\mathrm{D}(H), $$

where $\mathrm{L}(H)$ denotes the maximal number of self-loops attached to a vertex of $H$ . The bounds on $\tilde{\sigma},\sigma$ follows. Finally, note that $\sum_{e\in E_{H}}A_{e}g_{e}$ , where $(g_{e})_{e\in E_{H}}$ are i.i.d. standard real Gaussians, is a matrix with independent entries such that the variance of its $(i,j)$ entry for $i\leq j$ is the number of edges in $H$ between vertices $i$ and $j$ . The computation of $v$ follows immediately. ∎

Combining Proposition 9.1 and Lemma 9.6 yields an analogue of Theorem 3.13, in which $\varrho(\hat{H})$ is replaced by $\|X_{\mathrm{F}}\|$ . Moreover, Proposition 9.5 and (3.3) readily imply that $\|X_{\rm F}\|\leq(1+Cn^{-1}+C\mathrm{D}(H)^{-\frac{1}{4}})\varrho(\hat{H})$ . Thus the conclusion of Theorem 3.13 holds even when $H$ has self-loops, but with an extra $O(n^{-1})$ error term. However, when $H$ has no self-loops, the special structure of the coefficients $A_{e}$ enables us to eliminate the $O(n^{-1})$ term, so that the bound can be sharp even when $n\not\to\infty$ .

#### Lemma 9.7.

If $H$ has no self-loops, then

$$ \|X_{\rm F}\|\leq\bigg(1+\frac{C}{\mathrm{D}(H)^{\frac{1}{4}}}\bigg)\varrho(\hat{H}) $$

for a universal constant $C$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\varepsilon$ be as in Proposition 9.1. As $H$ is loopless, all $A_{e}$ are of the form $A=e_{i}e_{j}^{*}$ with $i<j$ . If we define $A_{\varepsilon}=(1-\varepsilon^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}A+\varepsilon A^{*}$ , then we can compute

$$ A_{\varepsilon}MA^{*}_{\varepsilon}+A^{*}_{\varepsilon}MA_{\varepsilon}=M_{jj}e_{i}e_{i}^{*}+M_{ii}e_{j}e_{j}^{*}+\frac{M_{ji}e_{i}e_{j}^{*}+M_{ij}e_{j}e_{i}^{*}}{n-1}. $$

The circular family $(c_{e})_{e\in E_{H}}$ can be realized as $c_{e}=l_{e}+\tilde{l}_{e}^{*}$ where $l_{e},\tilde{l}_{e}$ are canonical creation operators on a free Fock space [54, §1.2], we have [54, Theorem 1.3]

$$ \|X_{\rm F}\|=\inf_{M>0}\bigg\|M^{-1}+\sum_{e\in E_{H}}(A_{e\varepsilon}MA_{e\varepsilon}^{*}+A_{e\varepsilon}^{*}MA_{e\varepsilon})\bigg\|, $$

and moreover the infimum is attained by an $M$ so that the quantity inside the norm on the right-hand side is proportional to the identity. We can now reason precisely as in the proof of [9, Lemma 3.2] that the infimum in the above expression can be taken over diagonal matrices only. Therefore

$$ \|X_{\rm F}\|=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:x>0}\max_{i\in[d]}\bigg\{\frac{1}{x_{i}}+\sum_{j\in[d]:j\sim i}x_{j}\bigg\}, $$

where $j\sim i$ denotes that there is an edge between $i,j$ in $H$ . As the latter expression does not depend on $n$ , we can conclude that when $H$ has no self-loops, $\|X_{F}\|$ is unchanged if we set $\varepsilon=0$ . Then Proposition 9.5, (3.3), and Lemma 9.6 yield

$$ \|X_{\rm F}\|\leq\varrho(\hat{H})+C\mathrm{D}(H)^{\frac{1}{4}}. $$

It remains to note that $\varrho(\hat{H})\geq\mathrm{D}(H)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ by (3.3) and [66, eq. (9.7.2)]. ∎

We now conclude the proof of Theorem 3.13.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.13.

Applying Proposition 9.1 with $t=(a+2)\log nd$ yields
