$$ \mathbf{P}\bigg[\|X^{(n)\perp}\|\geq\bigg(1+C\frac{\mathrm{M}(H)^{\frac{1}{4}}}{n^{\frac{1}{4}}}\frac{(\log nd)^{\frac{3}{4}}}{\mathrm{D}(H)^{\frac{1}{4}}}+C\frac{(\log nd)^{\frac{2}{3}}}{\mathrm{D}(H)^{\frac{1}{6}}}+C\frac{\log nd}{\mathrm{D}(H)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\bigg)\varrho(\hat{H})\bigg]\leq(nd)^{-a} $$

using Lemmas 9.6 and 9.7, that $\varrho(\hat{H})\geq\mathrm{D}(H)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ as in the proof of Lemma 9.7, and that $\mathrm{M}(H)\leq\mathrm{D}(H)$ . Here $C$ is a constant that depends on $a$ only. ∎

### 9.2. Smallest singular value

The aim of this section is to prove Theorem 3.16. The proof is based on the following linearization lemma, which we state in a slightly more general form than is needed here as it will be used again in section 9.3.

#### Lemma 9.8.

Let $Y$ be a $d\times m$ random matrix, and let $B\geq 0$ be a nonrandom $m\times m$ positive semidefinite matrix. Define the $(d+2m)\times(d+2m)$ random matrix

$$ \hat{Y}_{\varepsilon}:=\begin{bmatrix}0&Y^{*}&(B+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
Y&0&0\\
(B+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}&0&0\end{bmatrix}, $$

and let $\hat{Y}_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{free}}$ be its noncommutative model. Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{sp}(\hat{Y}_{\varepsilon})\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(\hat{Y}_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{free}})+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\qquad\Longrightarrow \displaystyle\begin{cases}\lambda_{\rm max}(Y^{*}Y+B+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq\lambda_{\rm max}(Y_{\rm free}^{*}Y_{\rm free}+B\otimes\mathbf{1}+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}+\varepsilon,\\
\lambda_{\rm min}(Y^{*}Y+B+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}\geq\lambda_{\rm min}(Y_{\rm free}^{*}Y_{\rm free}+B\otimes\mathbf{1}+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}-\varepsilon\end{cases} $$

for any $\varepsilon\geq 0$ , where $\lambda_{\rm max}(X):=\sup\mathrm{sp}(X)$ and $\lambda_{\rm min}(X):=\inf\mathrm{sp}(X)$ .

#### Proof.

The proof is identical to that of [9, Lemma 3.13]. ∎

We can now complete the proof of Theorem 3.16.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.16.

We readily compute $\sigma_{*}(\hat{Y}_{\varepsilon})=\sigma_{*}(Y)$ , $\sigma(\hat{Y}_{\varepsilon})=\sigma(Y)$ , and $v(\hat{Y}_{\varepsilon})\leq\sqrt{2}\,v(Y)$ by [9, Lemma 4.10], while clearly $R(\hat{Y}_{\varepsilon})=R(Y)$ by Remark 2.1. Applying Theorem 2.16 and Lemma 9.8 with $B=0$ therefore yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\lambda_{\rm min}(Y^{*}Y+4\delta(t)^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq\lambda_{\rm min}(Y_{\rm free}^{*}Y_{\rm free}+4\delta(t)^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}-\delta(t)\big]\leq 6de^{-t}, $$

where

$$ \delta(t)=C\big\{v(Y)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(Y)^{\frac{1}{2}}(\log d)^{\frac{3}{4}}+\sigma_{*}(Y)\,t^{\frac{1}{2}}+R(Y)^{\frac{1}{3}}\sigma(Y)^{\frac{2}{3}}t^{\frac{2}{3}}+R(Y)\,t\big\} $$

for a universal constant $C$ . Using that $\lambda_{\rm min}(Y_{\rm free}^{*}Y_{\rm free}+4\delta(t)^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}\geq\mathrm{s_{min}}(Y_{\rm free})$ and $\lambda_{\rm min}(Y^{*}Y+4\delta(t)^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq\mathrm{s_{min}}(Y)+2\delta(t)$ , we obtain

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{s_{min}}(Y)\leq\mathrm{s_{min}}(Y_{\rm free})-3\delta(t)\big]\leq 6de^{-t}. $$

It remains to note that we can replace $6d$ by $d$ on the right-hand side if we increase the universal constant $C$ (as in the last step of the proof of Theorem 2.6). ∎

### 9.3. Sample covariance matrices

#### 9.3.1. Proof of Theorem 3.21

Gaussian random matrices are unbounded but possess moments of all orders. Therefore, a result along the lines of Theorem 3.21 can be proved either using Theorem 2.8 or using Theorem 2.9. These two approaches yield similar conclusions; we have chosen the latter approach here as it yields a slightly cleaner bound in the present setting. In preparation for the proof, let us estimate the relevant matrix parameters of the random matrix $S$ of (3.5).

#### Lemma 9.9.

We have

$$ \sigma(S)=\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big({\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[\Sigma_{i}]\Sigma_{i}+\Sigma_{i}^{2}}\big)\bigg\|^{\frac{1}{2}},\qquad v(S)\leq\sqrt{2}\,\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Sigma_{i}^{2}\bigg\|^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

The identity for $\sigma(S)$ follows readily using

$$ \mathbf{E}[(S-\mathbf{E}S)^{2}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}[(Y_{i}Y_{i}^{*}-\Sigma_{i})^{2}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(\mathbf{E}[Y_{i}Y_{i}^{*}\|Y_{i}\|^{2}]-\Sigma_{i}^{2}\big) $$

and that $\mathbf{E}[Y_{i}Y_{i}^{*}\|Y_{i}\|^{2}]=\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[\Sigma_{i}]\Sigma_{i}+2\Sigma_{i}^{2}$ by the Wick formula (4.1).

To bound $v(S)$ , we reason analogously. We first note that

$$ \mathbf{E}[|{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[M(S-\mathbf{E}S)]}|^{2}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(\mathbf{E}[|\langle Y_{i},MY_{i}\rangle|^{2}]-|{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[M\Sigma_{i}]}|^{2}\big)\leq 2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[M\Sigma_{i}M^{*}\Sigma_{i}], $$

using $\mathbf{E}[|\langle Y_{i},MY_{i}\rangle|^{2}]\leq|{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[M\Sigma_{i}]}|^{2}+2\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[M\Sigma_{i}M^{*}\Sigma_{i}]$ by (4.1) and Cauchy-Schwarz. As $2\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[M\Sigma_{i}M^{*}\Sigma_{i}]\leq 2\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[M\Sigma_{i}^{2}M^{*}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[\Sigma_{i}MM^{*}\Sigma_{i}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[(M^{*}M+MM^{*})\Sigma_{i}^{2}]$ by Cauchy-Schwarz and Young’s inequality, we have

$$ v(S)^{2}=\sup_{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}|M|^{2}\leq 1}\mathbf{E}[|{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[M(S-\mathbf{E}S)]}|^{2}]\leq\sup_{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}|M|^{2}\leq 1}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\bigg[(M^{*}M+MM^{*})\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Sigma_{i}^{2}\bigg], $$

and the conclusion follows readily. ∎

We must further estimate the parameter $R_{q}(S)$ in Theorem 2.9.

#### Lemma 9.10.

For $q\geq 1$ , we have $R_{q}(S)\lesssim n^{\frac{1}{q}}\max_{i\leq n}\{{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\Sigma_{i}+q\|\Sigma_{i}\|}\}$ .

#### Proof.

It follows directly from the definition of $R_{q}(S)$ that

$$ R_{q}(S)\leq n^{\frac{1}{q}}\max_{i\leq n}\mathbf{E}[\|Z_{i}\|^{q}]^{\frac{1}{q}}\leq 2n^{\frac{1}{q}}\max_{i\leq n}\mathbf{E}[\|Y_{i}\|^{2q}]^{\frac{1}{q}} $$

where we used $\|Z_{i}\|=\|Y_{i}Y_{i}^{*}-\mathbf{E}Y_{i}Y_{i}^{*}\|\leq\|Y_{i}\|^{2}+\mathbf{E}\|Y_{i}\|^{2}$ . It remains to note that

$$ \mathbf{E}[\|Y_{i}\|^{2q}]^{\frac{1}{2q}}\leq\mathbf{E}\|Y_{i}\|+\mathbf{E}[(\|Y_{i}\|-\mathbf{E}\|Y_{i}\|)^{2q}]^{\frac{1}{2q}}\lesssim(\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\Sigma_{i})^{\frac{1}{2}}+\|\Sigma_{i}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{q}, $$

where we used that $\mathbf{E}\|Y_{i}\|\leq(\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\Sigma_{i})^{\frac{1}{2}}$ by Cauchy-Schwarz and that $\|Y_{i}\|$ is $\|\Sigma_{i}\|$ -subgaussian by Gaussian concentration [22, Theorems 5.6 and 2.1]. ∎

We can now complete the proof of Theorem 3.21.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.21.

Theorem 2.9 and [9, Theorem 2.7 and Lemma 2.5] yield

$$ d^{-\frac{1}{2p}}\mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(S-\mathbf{E}S)^{2p}]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\leq 2\sigma(S)+Cv(S)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(S)^{\frac{1}{2}}p^{\frac{3}{4}}+CR_{2p}(S)p^{2} $$

for a universal constant $C$ . Now let $p=\lceil\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\log(d+n)\rceil$ , so that $\max(d^{\frac{1}{2p}},n^{\frac{1}{2p}})\leq e^{\frac{\varepsilon}{4}}$ . Moreover, $Cv(S)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(S)^{\frac{1}{2}}p^{\frac{3}{4}}\leq(e^{\frac{\varepsilon}{4}}-1)2\sigma(S)+\varepsilon^{-1}C^{2}v(S)p^{\frac{3}{2}}$ by Young’s inequality and $e^{x}\geq 1+x$ . We therefore obtain for any $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$

$$ \mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|\leq(1+\varepsilon)\,2\sigma(S)+\frac{K}{\varepsilon^{3}}\bigg(v(S)+\max_{i\leq n}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\Sigma_{i}\bigg)\log^{3}(d+n), $$

where $K$ is a universal constant and we used Lemma 9.10 and $e^{\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}\leq 1+\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon\leq 1$ . The conclusion follows readily using Lemma 9.9. ∎

#### 9.3.2. A simple lower bound

The aim of this short section is to show that the leading terms of the upper bounds of Theorems 3.20 and 3.21 are also lower bounds up to a universal constant. These results therefore capture the correct “user-friendly” quantity in the present setting. In general, it is not the case these these terms are optimal to leading order, that is up to a factor $1+o(1)$ ; if such a sharp bound is desired, the proofs of Theorems 3.20 and 3.21 may be adapted to obtain bounds in terms of $\|Y_{\rm free}Y_{\rm free}^{*}-\mathbf{E}S\otimes\mathbf{1}\|$ and $\|S_{\rm free}-\mathbf{E}S\otimes\mathbf{1}\|$ , respectively.

#### Lemma 9.11.

In the setting of section 3.4.1, we have

$$ \mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|\gtrsim\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[\Sigma_{i}]\Sigma_{i}\bigg\|^{\frac{1}{2}}+\max_{i\leq n}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\Sigma_{i}. $$

#### Proof.

We begin by noting that

$$ \mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|\geq\sup_{\|v\|=1}\mathbf{E}\|(S-\mathbf{E}S)v\|\gtrsim\sup_{\|v\|=1}\mathbf{E}[\|(S-\mathbf{E}S)v\|^{2}]^{\frac{1}{2}}, $$

where the last inequality follows by hypercontractivity [49, Theorem 3.50] using that $\|(S-\mathbf{E}S)v\|^{2}$ is a polynomial of degree $4$ of the Gaussian variables $Y_{ij}$ . The first part of the proof of Lemma 9.9 therefore yields

$$ \mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|\gtrsim\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big({\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[\Sigma_{i}]\Sigma_{i}+\Sigma_{i}^{2}}\big)\bigg\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\geq\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[\Sigma_{i}]\Sigma_{i}\bigg\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\geq\max_{i\leq n}\|\Sigma_{i}\|. $$

On the other hand, we can readily estimate by Jensen’s inequality

$$ \mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|\geq\max_{i\leq n}\mathbf{E}\|Y_{i}Y_{i}^{*}-\Sigma_{i}\|\geq\max_{i\leq n}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\Sigma_{i}-\max_{i\leq n}\|\Sigma_{i}\|, $$

where we used that $S-\mathbf{E}S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_{i}Y_{i}^{*}-\Sigma_{i})$ is a sum of independent centered random matrices. We can therefore estimate

$$ \bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[\Sigma_{i}]\Sigma_{i}\bigg\|^{\frac{1}{2}}+\max_{i\leq n}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\Sigma_{i}\leq\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[\Sigma_{i}]\Sigma_{i}\bigg\|^{\frac{1}{2}}+\max_{i\leq n}\|\Sigma_{i}\|+\mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|, $$

and the proof is readily concluded. ∎

#### 9.3.3. Proof of Theorem 3.24

The proof of Theorem 3.24 combines our universality principles with a linearization argument as in Lemma 9.8.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.24.

Given $B=\|\mathbf{E}YY^{*}\|\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{E}YY^{*}$ , define

$$ \breve{Y}_{\varepsilon}:=\begin{bmatrix}0&Y&(B+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
Y^{*}&0&0\\
(B+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}&0&0\end{bmatrix}, $$

and let $\breve{H}_{\varepsilon}$ be its Gaussian model. Then a completely analogous argument to the one used in the proof of Lemma 9.8 yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(\breve{Y}_{\varepsilon}),\mathrm{sp}(\breve{H}_{\varepsilon}))\leq\varepsilon\qquad\Longrightarrow \displaystyle\begin{cases}\big|\lambda_{\rm max}(YY^{*}+B+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}-\lambda_{\rm max}(HH^{*}+B+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}\big|\leq\varepsilon,\\
\big|\lambda_{\rm min}(YY^{*}+B+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}-\lambda_{\rm min}(HH^{*}+B+4\varepsilon^{2}\mathbf{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}\big|\leq\varepsilon\end{cases} $$

for any $\varepsilon\geq 0$ . Using $|a^{\frac{1}{2}}-b^{\frac{1}{2}}|(a^{\frac{1}{2}}+b^{\frac{1}{2}})=|a-b|$ for $a,b\geq 0$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(\breve{Y}_{\varepsilon}),\mathrm{sp}(\breve{H}_{\varepsilon}))\leq\varepsilon\qquad\Longrightarrow \displaystyle\big|\|YY^{*}-\mathbf{E}YY^{*}\|-\|HH^{*}-\mathbf{E}HH^{*}\|\big|\leq\big(\|Y\|+\|H\|+2\|\mathbf{E}YY^{*}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}+4\varepsilon\big)\varepsilon, $$

where we used that $|\|M\|-\|N\||\leq|\lambda_{\rm max}(M)-\lambda_{\rm max}(N)|\vee|\lambda_{\rm min}(M)-\lambda_{\rm min}(N)|$ and $\mathbf{E}HH^{*}=\mathbf{E}YY^{*}$ . Furthermore, we have $\sigma_{*}(\breve{Y}_{\varepsilon})=\sigma_{*}(Y)$ , $\sigma(\breve{Y}_{\varepsilon})=\sigma(Y)$ , and $R(\breve{Y}_{\varepsilon})=R(Y)$ by [9, Remark 2.6]. Thus Theorem 2.6 yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\big|\|YY^{*}-\mathbf{E}YY^{*}\|-\|HH^{*}-\mathbf{E}HH^{*}\|\big|>\\
C\big(\|Y\|+\|H\|+\|\mathbf{E}YY^{*}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}+\varepsilon(t)\big)\varepsilon(t)\big]\leq(2d+m)e^{-t} $$

for all $t>0$ , where $C$ is a universal constant and $\varepsilon(t)$ is as in Theorem 2.6.

To proceed, note that

$$ \mathbf{P}[\|H\|>\mathbf{E}\|H\|+C\varepsilon(t)]\leq e^{-t} $$

by Gaussian concentration as in [9, Corollary 4.14], while

$$ \mathbf{P}[\|Y\|>\mathbf{E}\|H\|+C\varepsilon(t)]\leq(d+m)e^{-t} $$

by Corollary 2.7 and Remark 2.1. Combining the above bounds yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\big|\|YY^{*}-\mathbf{E}YY^{*}\|-\|HH^{*}-\mathbf{E}HH^{*}\|\big|>C\varepsilon(t)\,\mathbf{E}\|H\|+C\varepsilon(t)^{2}\big]\leq C(d+m)e^{-t} $$

for a universal constant $C$ , where we used that

$$ \|\mathbf{E}YY^{*}\|=\|\mathbf{E}HH^{*}\|=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\mathbf{E}\|H^{*}v\|^{2}\lesssim\sup_{\|v\|=1}(\mathbf{E}\|H^{*}v\|)^{2}\leq(\mathbf{E}\|H\|)^{2} $$

by hypercontractivity [49, Theorem 3.50]. The conclusion follows by integrating this tail bound as in the proof of Theorem 2.6. ∎

#### 9.3.4. Proof of Theorem 3.27

Throughout this section we adopt the setting and notation of Theorem 3.27. Its proof combines two distinct universality principles. Let us begin by applying universality to $Y$ .

#### Proposition 9.12.

We have

$$ \mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|\leq 2\|B\|_{\rm HS}\|B\|\sqrt{n}+\|B\|_{\rm HS}^{2}\\
+C\big\{\alpha^{\frac{1}{3}}\|B\|^{\frac{1}{3}}(\|B\|\sqrt{n}+\|B\|_{\rm HS})^{\frac{5}{3}}+\alpha^{2}\|B\|^{2}\big\}\log^{2}(d+n). $$

#### Proof.

We will write $Y$ in the form (2.1) as

$$ Y=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Z_{ij},\qquad Z_{ij}=A_{ij}\,Be_{i}e_{j}^{*}. $$

We readily compute

$$ \mathbf{E}[YY^{*}]=n\,BB^{*},\qquad\mathbf{E}[Y^{*}Y]=\|B\|_{\rm HS}^{2}\mathbf{1},\qquad v(Y)=\|B\|,\qquad R(Y)\leq\alpha\|B\| $$

(here we used that $Y$ has independent columns $Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n}$ with $\mathrm{Cov}(Y_{i})=BB^{*}$ , so that $\|\mathrm{Cov}(Y)\|=\max_{i}\|\mathrm{Cov}(Y_{i})\|=\|B\|^{2}$ ). Applying Theorem 3.24 yields

$$ \big|\mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|-\mathbf{E}\|HH^{*}-\mathbf{E}HH^{*}\|\big|\lesssim\delta\,(\|B\|\sqrt{n}+\|B\|_{\rm HS})+\delta^{2}, $$

where

$$ \delta\lesssim\alpha^{\frac{1}{3}}\|B\|^{\frac{1}{3}}(\|B\|\sqrt{n}+\|B\|_{\rm HS})^{\frac{2}{3}}\log^{\frac{2}{3}}(d+n)+\alpha\|B\|\log(d+n) $$

and we used that $\mathbf{E}\|H\|\lesssim\|B\|\sqrt{n}+\|B\|_{\rm HS}$ (see, e.g., [80, Lemma 5.4]) and $\alpha\geq 1$ . On the other hand, $\mathbf{E}\|HH^{*}-\mathbf{E}HH^{*}\|$ can be estimated by Theorem 3.20 with $\Sigma_{i}=BB^{*}$ . Combining all the above bounds yields the conclusion. ∎

We now apply universality to $S$ . In preparation for the following computations, we begin by estimating $\sigma(S)$ and $v(S)$ . Recall that $Y_{i}$ denotes the $i$ th column of $Y$ .

#### Lemma 9.13.

We have

$$ \sigma(S)\leq(\|B\|_{\rm HS}\|B\|+2\alpha\|B\|^{2})\sqrt{n},\qquad v(S)\leq 4\alpha\|B\|^{2}\sqrt{n}. $$

#### Proof.

By Lemma 4.1, if $W_{1},\ldots,W_{m}$ are independent centered random variables with unit variance and $g_{1},\ldots,g_{m}$ are independent standard Gaussians, then

$$ \mathbf{E}[W_{i}W_{j}W_{k}W_{l}]=\mathbf{E}[g_{i}g_{j}g_{k}g_{l}]+(\mathbf{E}[W_{i}^{4}]-3)1_{i=j=k=l}. $$

We will apply this identity in the case that $W_{i}$ are entries of the random matrix $A$ . In particular, arguing as in the first part of the proof of Lemma 9.9, we obtain

$$ \mathbf{E}[(S-\mathbf{E}S)^{2}]=n\|B\|_{\rm HS}^{2}BB^{*}+n(BB^{*})^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(\mathbf{E}[A_{ij}^{4}]-3)(B^{*}B)_{ii}Be_{i}e_{i}^{*}B^{*}. $$

As $\mathbf{E}[A_{ij}^{4}]\leq\alpha^{2}$ , we readily obtain

$$ \sigma(S)^{2}\leq n\|B\|_{\rm HS}^{2}\|B\|^{2}+(1+\alpha^{2})n\|B\|^{4}, $$

and the bound on $\sigma(S)$ follows using $\alpha\geq 1$ .

The parameter $v(S)$ can be estimated analogously, but an adequate bound also follows from a standard concentration argument. Indeed, note that

$$ v(S)^{2}=\sup_{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}|M|^{2}=1}\mathrm{Var}({\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}MS})=\sup_{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}|M|^{2}=1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Var}(\langle Y_{i},MY_{i}\rangle). $$

By the convex Poincaré inequality [22, Theorem 3.17] and Cauchy-Schwarz, we obtain $\mathrm{Var}(\langle Y_{i},MY_{i}\rangle)\leq 16\alpha^{2}\|B\|^{4}$ for $\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}|M|^{2}=1$ , concluding the proof. ∎

Next, we estimate the parameter $R_{q}(S)$ in Theorem 2.9.

#### Lemma 9.14.

For $q\geq 1$ , we have $R_{q}(S)\lesssim n^{\frac{1}{q}}\{\|B\|_{\rm HS}^{2}+\alpha^{2}q\|B\|^{2}\}$ .

#### Proof.

The convex concentration inequality [22, Theorems 6.10 and 2.1] yields that $\mathbf{E}[\|Y_{i}\|^{2q}]^{\frac{1}{2q}}\leq\|B\|_{\rm HS}+C\alpha\sqrt{q}\|B\|$ , where we used $\mathbf{E}\|Y_{i}\|\leq\mathbf{E}[\|Y_{i}\|^{2}]^{\frac{1}{2}}=\|B\|_{\rm HS}$ . The conclusion follows directly as in the proof of Lemma 9.10. ∎

We can now proceed as in the proof of Theorem 3.21.

#### Proposition 9.15.

We have for $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$

$$ \mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|\leq(1+\varepsilon)\,2\|B\|_{\rm HS}\|B\|\sqrt{n}+\frac{C}{\varepsilon^{3}}\big(\|B\|_{\rm HS}^{2}+(\alpha\sqrt{n}+\alpha^{2})\|B\|^{2}\big)\log^{3}(d+n). $$

#### Proof.

Apply Lemmas 9.13 and 9.14 precisely as in the proof of Theorem 3.21. ∎

We now complete the proof of Theorem 3.27.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.27.

It is convenient to define $\gamma=\frac{\|B\|_{\rm HS}}{\|B\|\sqrt{n}}$ and $\delta=\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{n}}$ . In terms of these dimensionless parameters, Proposition 9.12 can be expressed as

$$ \frac{\mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|}{n\|B\|^{2}}\leq 2\gamma+\gamma^{2}+C\big\{\delta^{\frac{1}{3}}(1+\gamma)^{\frac{5}{3}}+\delta^{2}\big\}\log^{2}(d+n) $$

while Proposition 9.15 yields

$$ \frac{\mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|}{n\|B\|^{2}}\leq 2\gamma+C\big\{(\gamma^{2}+\delta+\delta^{2})^{\frac{1}{4}}\gamma^{\frac{3}{4}}+\gamma^{2}+\delta+\delta^{2}\big\}\log^{3}(d+n), $$

where in the last equation we used $\inf_{\varepsilon\leq 1}\{2\varepsilon\gamma+\frac{K}{\varepsilon^{3}}\}\leq 3K^{\frac{1}{4}}\gamma^{\frac{3}{4}}+3K$ .

Now note that the assumptions of the theorem imply $\delta\leq 1$ and $\gamma\geq\delta$ . Using $\delta^{2}\leq\delta^{\frac{1}{3}}(1+\gamma)^{\frac{5}{3}}$ , $\frac{\delta^{\frac{1}{3}}(1+\gamma)^{\frac{5}{3}}}{2\gamma+\gamma^{2}}\lesssim\frac{\delta^{\frac{1}{3}}}{\gamma}+(\frac{\delta}{\gamma})^{\frac{1}{3}}$ and $\frac{\delta}{\gamma}\leq 1$ , we can rearrange and combine the above inequalities to estimate

$$ \frac{\mathbf{E}\|S-\mathbf{E}S\|}{n\|B\|^{2}}\leq\bigg(1+C\bigg\{\min\bigg(\frac{\delta^{\frac{1}{3}}}{\gamma},\gamma^{\frac{1}{4}}+\gamma\bigg)+\frac{\delta^{\frac{1}{4}}}{\gamma^{\frac{1}{4}}}\bigg\}\log^{3}(d+n)\bigg)(2\gamma+\gamma^{2}). $$

We conclude with $\min(\frac{a}{\gamma},\gamma^{\frac{1}{4}}+\gamma)\leq\min(\frac{a}{\gamma},\gamma^{\frac{1}{4}})+\min(\frac{a}{\gamma},\gamma)\leq a^{\frac{1}{5}}+a^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $\delta<1$ . ∎

#### Remark 9.16 (Unbounded entries).

The formulation of Theorem 3.27 for bounded $A_{ij}$ is not a fundamental restriction of our approach: results for unbounded entries can be obtained analogously by using our universality principles for unbounded random matrices. We have restricted to the bounded case largely for simplicity and brevity of exposition. However, in order to illustrate some features of the unbounded case, let us briefly discuss these here in the context of the slightly simpler problem of estimating $\|Y\|$ (as opposed to $\|YY^{*}-\mathbf{E}YY^{*}\|$ ).

Let $Y=BA$ with $A,B$ as in Theorem 3.27, except that we now assume only that $\|A_{ij}\|_{s}\leq\alpha$ for some $4<s<\infty$ . We write $Y$ in the form (2.1) as in the proof of Proposition 9.12. Applying Theorem 2.8 as in the proof of Corollary 2.17 yields

$$ \mathbf{E}\|Y\|\leq\|\mathbf{E}YY^{*}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}+\|\mathbf{E}Y^{*}Y\|^{\frac{1}{2}}+C\big\{v(Y)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sigma(Y)^{\frac{1}{2}}+\bar{R}(Y)^{\frac{1}{6}}\sigma(Y)^{\frac{5}{6}}\big\}\log(d+n) $$

provided that $\bar{R}(Y)\log^{3}(d+n)\leq\sigma(Y)$ . All parameters in this bound were already computed in the proof of Proposition 9.12 except $\bar{R}(Y)$ , which we estimate as

$$ \displaystyle\bar{R}(Y) \displaystyle=\mathbf{E}\bigg[\max_{i\leq N}\max_{j\leq n}A_{ij}^{2}\|Be_{i}\|^{2}\bigg]^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq\mathbf{E}\bigg[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|A_{ij}|^{s}\|Be_{i}\|^{s}\bigg]^{\frac{1}{s}} \displaystyle\leq\alpha n^{\frac{1}{s}}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|Be_{i}\|^{s}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{s}}\leq\alpha n^{\frac{1}{s}}\|B\|^{1-\frac{2}{s}}\|B\|_{\rm HS}^{\frac{2}{s}}. $$

Combining the above estimates, we obtain the bound

$$ \mathbf{E}\|Y\|\leq\bigg(1+\frac{C\log(d+n)}{(n\vee r)^{\frac{1}{4}}}+\frac{C\alpha^{\frac{1}{6}}\log(d+n)}{(n\vee r)^{\frac{1}{12}-\frac{1}{3s}}}\bigg)\big(\|B\|\sqrt{n}+\|B\|_{\rm HS}\big) $$

for $\alpha\log^{3}(d+n)\leq(n\vee r)^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{2}{s}}$ , where $r=\|B\|_{\rm HS}^{2}\|B\|^{-2}$ is the effective rank of $B$ and we used that $\|B\|\sqrt{n}+\|B\|_{\rm HS}\geq(\|B\|\sqrt{n})^{1-t}\|B\|_{\rm HS}^{t}$ for any $t\in[0,1]$ .

This result should be compared to the best previous bound in this setting due to Vershynin [82], which states that $\mathbf{E}\|Y\|\leq C(s)\alpha(\|B\|\sqrt{n}+\|B\|_{\rm HS})$ where $C(s)<\infty$ for $s>4$ . In contrast, our bound yields $\mathbf{E}\|Y\|\leq(1+o(1))(\|B\|\sqrt{n}+\|B\|_{\rm HS})$ as soon as $n\vee r\gg(\alpha^{\frac{1}{6}}\log(d+n))^{\beta(s)}$ , which not only yields the best possible constant for a bound of this kind (in view of the Bai-Yin law) but also allows $\alpha$ to diverge without affecting the estimate to leading order. We emphasize a key feature of both bounds that was highlighted in [82]: they do not depend on the inner dimension $N$ , despite that $\bar{R}(Y)$ is defined as a maximum over $nN$ random variables.

### 9.4. Strong asymptotic freeness

The main aim of this section is to prove Theorem 3.29. In section 9.4.1, we first develop the special case of bounded random matrices by means of a linearization argument. The result is then extended to the general setting in section 9.4.2 by employing a truncation argument as in section 8. Finally, Corollary 3.32 will be proved in section 9.4.3.

#### 9.4.1. Linearization

The aim of this section is to prove the following special case of Theorem 3.29 for bounded random matrices. The general case will be deduced from this result in the next section by a truncation argument.

#### Theorem 9.17.

Let $s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}$ be a free semicircular family, and let $H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{m}^{N}$ be independent self-adjoint random matrices as in Theorem 3.29. Suppose

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\|\mathbf{E}[H_{k}^{N}]\|=\lim_{N\to\infty}\|\mathbf{E}[(H_{k}^{N})^{2}]-\mathbf{1}\|=0 $$

and

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}(\log d_{N})^{\frac{3}{2}}v(H_{k}^{N})=\lim_{N\to\infty}(\log d_{N})^{2}R(H_{k}^{N})=0 $$

for every $1\leq k\leq m$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}p(H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{m}^{N})=\tau(p(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}))\quad\mbox{a.s.}, \displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty}\|p(H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{m}^{N})\|=\|p(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})\|\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

for every noncommutative polynomial $p$ .

The difficulty here is that we are interested in general noncommutative polynomials of random matrices, while our universality principles apply only to the linear situation of (2.1). To reduce the former to the latter, we will use classical linearization arguments that we presently recall.

#### Proposition 9.18 (Linearization).

Let $H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{m}^{N}$ be self-adjoint random matrices and let $s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}$ be a free semicircular family.

- a. Suppose that for every $d^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}$ and $A_{0},\ldots,A_{m}\in\mathrm{M}_{d^{\prime}}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}$

$$ \mathrm{sp}\big(A_{0}\otimes\mathbf{1}+\textstyle{\sum_{k=1}^{m}}A_{k}\otimes H_{k}^{N}\big)\subseteq\mathrm{sp}\big(A_{0}\otimes\mathbf{1}+\textstyle{\sum_{k=1}^{m}}A_{k}\otimes s_{k}\big)+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon] $$

eventually as $N\to\infty$ a.s. for all $\varepsilon>0$ . Then

$$ \limsup_{N\to\infty}\|p(H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{m}^{N})\|\leq\|p(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})\|\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

for every noncommutative polynomial $p$ .

- b. Suppose that for every $d^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}$ and $A_{0},\ldots,A_{m}\in\mathrm{M}_{d^{\prime}}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}$

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\big[\big(A_{0}\otimes\mathbf{1}+\textstyle{\sum_{k=1}^{m}}A_{k}\otimes H_{k}^{N}\big)^{2r}\big]=({\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}}\otimes\tau)\big[\big(A_{0}\otimes\mathbf{1}+\textstyle{\sum_{k=1}^{m}}A_{k}\otimes s_{k}\big)^{2r}\big] $$

a.s. for all $r\in\mathbb{N}$ . Then

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}p(H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{k}^{N})=\tau(p(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}))\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

for every noncommutative polynomial $p$ .

#### Proof.

The first part is proved in [47, Lemma 1 and pp. 758–760]. The second part follows directly from the proof of [38, Lemma 1.1]. ∎

To apply the linearization argument in the present setting, we use the following.

#### Lemma 9.19.

Let $H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{m}^{N}$ be random matrices as in Theorem 9.17, and fix $d^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}$ and $A_{0},\ldots,A_{m}\in\mathrm{M}_{d^{\prime}}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}$ . Define the random matrix

$$ \Xi^{N}=A_{0}\otimes\mathbf{1}+\sum_{k=1}^{m}A_{k}\otimes H_{k}^{N}, $$

and let $\Xi^{N}_{\rm free}$ be the associated noncommutative model. Then

$$ \mathrm{sp}(\Xi^{N})\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(\Xi^{N}_{\rm free})+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon] $$

eventually as $N\to\infty$ a.s. for every $\varepsilon>0$ , and for every $r\in\mathbb{N}$

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\big|{\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[(\Xi^{N})^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}-({\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}}\otimes\tau)[(\Xi^{N}_{\rm free})^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}}\big|=0\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

#### Proof.

It follows as in the proof of [9, Lemma 7.8] that $\sigma(\Xi^{N})=O(1)$ and $\sigma_{*}(\Xi^{N})\leq v(\Xi^{N})=o((\log d_{N})^{-\frac{3}{2}})$ . Moreover, it is clear from the definition of $\Xi^{N}$ that

$$ R(\Xi^{N})=\max_{k\leq m}\|A_{k}\|R(H_{k}^{N})=o((\log d_{N})^{-2}). $$

Applying Theorem 2.16 with $t=3\log d_{N}$ yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{sp}(\Xi^{N})\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(\Xi^{N}_{\rm free})+o(1)[-1,1]\big]\geq 1-\frac{2d^{\prime}}{d_{N}^{2}}\geq 1-\frac{2d^{\prime}}{N^{2}}. $$

The first conclusion follows by the Borel-Cantelli lemma.

On the other hand, Theorem 2.9 and [9, Theorem 2.7] yield for all $r\in\mathbb{N}$

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\big|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\Xi^{N})^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}-({\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}}\otimes\tau)[(\Xi^{N}_{\rm free})^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}\big|=0. $$

In particular, $\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\Xi^{N})^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}=O(1)$ as $({\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}}\otimes\tau)[(\Xi^{N}_{\rm free})^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}\leq\|\Xi^{N}_{\rm free}\|\leq 2\sigma(\Xi^{N})$ . To conclude, we need to show that $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[(\Xi^{N})^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}$ concentrates around $\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\Xi^{N})^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}$ a.s. To this end, we apply Lemma 9.20 below with $t=2\log d_{N}$ to estimate

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\big|{\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[(\Xi^{N})^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}-\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\Xi^{N})^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}}\big|\geq o(1)\big]\leq\frac{1}{d_{N}^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{N^{2}}, $$

and the conclusion follows by Borel-Cantelli. ∎

Above we used the following concentration inequality.

#### Lemma 9.20.

For any random matrix as in (2.1), we have

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\big|(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2r})^{\frac{1}{2r}}-\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}\big|\geq C\big(\sigma_{*}(X)+R(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{4r}}\big)\sqrt{t}+CR(X)t\big]\leq 2e^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq r$ .

#### Proof.

We begin by writing $(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2r})^{\frac{1}{2r}}=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\big|\sum_{i=0}^{n}f(Z_{i})\big|$ where

$$ \mathcal{F}=\{Z\mapsto x\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[MZ]+y\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}[MZ]:x^{2}+y^{2}\leq 1,\|M\|_{\frac{2r}{2r-1}}\leq 1\}. $$

Then

$$ \sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\mathrm{Var}(f(Z_{i}))\leq\sup_{\|M\|_{1}\leq 1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}|{\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}MZ_{i}}|^{2}=\sigma_{*}(X)^{2} $$

as $\|M\|_{1}\leq\|M\|_{\frac{2r}{2r-1}}$ and as the extreme points of $S_{1}^{d}$ are rank one matrices, and

$$ \sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\max_{0\leq i\leq n}\|f(Z_{i})-f(Z_{i}^{\prime})\|_{\infty}\leq 2R(X) $$

where $Z_{i}^{\prime}$ is an independent copy of $Z_{i}$ . We now apply55 5 While the statement of [57, Theorem 3] assumes that $\|f\|_{\infty}\leq b$ for all $f\in\mathcal{F}$ , only the weaker assumption $\|f(\xi_{i})-f(\xi_{i}^{\prime})\|_{\infty}\leq 2b$ is used in the proof. We also optimized the conclusion over $\varepsilon$ . [57, Theorem 3] to estimate

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\big|(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2r})^{\frac{1}{2r}}-\mathbf{E}[(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2r})^{\frac{1}{2r}}]\big|\geq\\
C\big(\sigma_{*}(X)+R(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{E}[(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2r})^{\frac{1}{2r}}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\big)\sqrt{t}+CR(X)t\big]\leq 2e^{-t} $$

for all $t\geq 0$ . Consequently

$$ \big|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2r}]^{\frac{1}{2r}}-\mathbf{E}[(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2r})^{\frac{1}{2r}}]\big|\lesssim\big(\sigma_{*}(X)+R(X)^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{E}[(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}X^{2r})^{\frac{1}{2r}}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\big)\sqrt{r}+R(X)r $$

by [22, Theorem 2.3], and we conclude by combining the above inequalities. ∎

We can now conclude the proof of Theorem 9.17.

#### Proof of Theorem 9.17.

Let $\Xi^{N}$ and $\Xi^{N}_{\rm free}$ be as in Lemma 9.19. It follows from the proofs of [9, Lemmas 7.9 and 7.10] that

$$ \mathrm{sp}(\Xi^{N}_{\rm free})\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(\textstyle{A_{0}\otimes\mathbf{1}+\sum_{k=1}^{m}A_{k}\otimes s_{k}})+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon] $$

eventually as $N\to\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$ , and that

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}({\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}}\otimes\tau)[(\Xi^{N}_{\rm free})^{2r}]=({\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}}\otimes\tau)[(\textstyle{A_{0}\otimes\mathbf{1}+\sum_{k=1}^{m}A_{k}\otimes s_{k}})^{2r}] $$

for all $r\in\mathbb{N}$ . Thus Lemma 9.19 and Proposition 9.18 yield

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}p(H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{m}^{N})=\tau(p(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}))\quad\mbox{a.s.}, \displaystyle\limsup_{N\to\infty}\|p(H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{m}^{N})\|\leq\|p(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})\|\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

for every noncommutative polynomial $p$ . To conclude, note that

$$ \displaystyle\liminf_{N\to\infty}\|p(H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{m}^{N})\| \displaystyle\geq\liminf_{N\to\infty}(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}|p(H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{m}^{N})|^{2r})^{\frac{1}{2r}} \displaystyle=\tau(|p(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})|^{2r})^{\frac{1}{2r}}\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

for any $r\in\mathbb{N}$ , where we used that $|p|^{2r}$ is also a polynomial. As

$$ \lim_{r\to\infty}\tau(|p(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})|^{2r})^{\frac{1}{2r}}=\|p(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})\| $$

(here we use that $\tau$ is faithful), the conclusion follows. ∎

#### 9.4.2. Proof of Theorem 3.29

To prove Theorem 3.29 in the general setting, we will combine Theorem 9.17 with the truncation arguments of section 8. Before we proceed to the proof, we state an elementary lemma that will be needed below.

#### Lemma 9.21.

Let $(Y_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables such that $|Y_{n}|\to 0$ a.s. as $n\to\infty$ . Then there is a nonrandom sequence $(a_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ with $a_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ , such that $|Y_{n}|\leq a_{n}$ eventually as $n\to\infty$ a.s.

#### Proof.

Let $Y_{n}^{*}:=\sup_{m\geq n}|Y_{m}|$ , and let $n_{k}:=\inf\{n:\mathbf{P}[Y_{n}^{*}>2^{-k}]\leq 2^{-k}]\}$ . Then clearly $n_{k}$ is nondecreasing, and $n_{k}<\infty$ as we assumed $|Y_{n}|\to 0$ a.s. Moreover, we may assume without loss of generality that $n_{k}\to\infty$ , as otherwise $Y_{n}^{*}=0$ a.s. for some $n$ and the conclusion is trivial. We may therefore define $(a_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ by setting $a_{n}=2^{-k}$ for $n_{k}\leq n<n_{k+1}$ , $k\geq 0$ . As by construction

$$ \mathbf{P}[|Y_{n}|>a_{n}\mbox{ for some }n_{k}\leq n<n_{k+1}]\leq\mathbf{P}[Y_{n_{k}}^{*}>2^{-k}]\leq 2^{-k}, $$

the conclusion follows by the Borel-Cantelli lemma. ∎

We can now complete the proof of Theorem 3.29.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.29.

We first note that it suffices to prove the a.s. version of the theorem, as the in probability version follows immediately from the a.s. version using the classical fact that a sequence of random variables converges in probability if and only if every subsequence has an a.s. convergent subsequence.

We therefore assume from now on that the assumptions of the theorem hold in the a.s. sense. By Lemma 9.21, the assumptions imply that there exists a nonrandom sequence $(a_{N})$ with $a_{N}\to 0$ as $N\to\infty$ such that

$$ \max_{1\leq k\leq m}\max_{1\leq i\leq M_{N}}\|Z_{ki}^{N}\|\leq(\log d_{N})^{-2}a_{N} $$

eventually as $N\to\infty$ a.s. Now define the truncated random matrices

$$ \tilde{H}_{k}^{N}:=Z_{k0}^{N}+\sum_{i=1}^{M_{N}}1_{\|Z_{ki}^{N}\|\leq(\log d_{N})^{-2}a_{N}}Z_{ki}^{N} $$

as in section 8. Then $\tilde{H}_{k}^{N}=H_{k}^{N}$ eventually as $N\to\infty$ a.s. for all $k$ . To complete the proof, it therefore suffices to show that $\tilde{H}_{1}^{N},\ldots,\tilde{H}_{m}^{N}$ satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 9.17. To this end, note first that by Lemma 8.6

$$ (\log d_{N})^{2}R(\tilde{H}_{k}^{N})\leq 2a_{N}\xrightarrow{N\to\infty}0. $$

Using $\mathbf{E}[|1_{A}Y-\mathbf{E}[1_{A}Y]|^{2}]\leq\mathbf{E}[|Y|^{2}]$ as in the proof of Lemma 8.6, we also have

$$ (\log d_{N})^{\frac{3}{2}}v(\tilde{H}_{k}^{N})\leq(\log d_{N})^{\frac{3}{2}}v(H_{k}^{N})\xrightarrow{N\to\infty}0. $$

It remains to estimate $\mathbf{E}[\tilde{H}_{k}^{N}]$ and $\mathbf{E}[(\tilde{H}_{k}^{N})^{2}]$ .

To bound $\mathbf{E}[\tilde{H}_{k}^{N}]$ , note that it was shown in the proof of Lemma 8.4 that

$$ \|\mathbf{E}[\tilde{H}_{k}^{N}]-\mathbf{E}[H_{k}^{N}]\|\leq\frac{\sigma_{*}(H_{k}^{N})}{\mathbf{P}[\max_{j}\|Z_{kj}^{N}\|\leq(\log d_{N})^{-2}a_{N}]^{\frac{1}{2}}}. $$

But as $\max_{j}\|Z_{kj}^{N}\|\leq(\log d_{N})^{-2}a_{N}$ eventually a.s., the denominator on the right-hand side converges to one and the numerator satisfies $\sigma_{*}(H_{k}^{N})\leq v(H_{k}^{N})\to 0$ . As by assumption $\|\mathbf{E}[H_{k}^{N}]\|\to 0$ , we conclude that $\|\mathbf{E}[\tilde{H}_{k}^{N}]\|\to 0$ as well.

To bound $\mathbf{E}[(\tilde{H}_{k}^{N})^{2}]$ , note that setting $M=\mathbf{1}$ in the proof of Lemma 8.5 yields

$$ \|\mathbf{E}[(\tilde{H}_{k}^{N}-\mathbf{E}\tilde{H}_{k}^{N})^{2}]-\mathbf{E}[(H_{k}^{N}-\mathbf{E}H_{k}^{N})^{2}]\|\\
\leq 2\,\mathbf{P}[{\textstyle\max_{j}\|Z_{kj}^{N}\|>(\log d_{N})^{-2}a_{N}}]\,\sigma(H_{k}^{N})^{2}+4\,\bar{R}(H_{k}^{N})\sigma(H_{k}^{N}). $$

The right-hand side converges to zero as $\max_{j}\|Z_{kj}^{N}\|\leq(\log d_{N})^{-2}a_{N}$ eventually a.s. and as $\bar{R}(H_{k}^{N})\to 0$ and $\sigma(H_{k}^{N})=O(1)$ by assumption. As $\|\mathbf{E}[\tilde{H}_{k}^{N}]\|\to 0$ , $\|\mathbf{E}[H_{k}^{N}]\|\to 0$ , and $\|\mathbf{E}[(H_{k}^{N})^{2}]-\mathbf{1}\|\to 0$ , we conclude that $\|\mathbf{E}[(\tilde{H}_{k}^{N})^{2}]-\mathbf{1}\|\to 0$ . ∎

#### 9.4.3. Proof of Corollary 3.32

Before we proceed to the proof of Corollary 3.32, we first state another elementary probabilistic lemma.

#### Lemma 9.22.

Let $(Y_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with $\mathbf{E}[|Y_{n}|^{p}]<\infty$ for some $p>0$ . Then $\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-\frac{1}{p}}\max_{m\leq n}|Y_{m}|=0$ a.s.

#### Proof.

By the union bound and as $\sum_{k\geq 0}2^{k}1_{2^{k}\leq x}\leq 2x$ , we can estimate

$$ \sum_{k\geq 0}\mathbf{P}\bigg[2^{-\frac{k}{p}}\max_{m\leq 2^{k}}|Y_{m}|\geq\varepsilon\bigg]\leq\sum_{k\geq 0}2^{k}\,\mathbf{P}\bigg[|Y_{1}|^{p}\geq 2^{k}\varepsilon^{p}\bigg]\leq\frac{2\,\mathbf{E}[|Y_{1}|^{p}]}{\varepsilon^{p}}<\infty $$

for any $\varepsilon>0$ . Thus

$$ \lim_{k\to\infty}\max_{2^{k-1}\leq n<2^{k}}n^{-\frac{1}{p}}\max_{m\leq n}|Y_{m}|\leq 2^{\frac{1}{p}}\lim_{k\to\infty}2^{-\frac{k}{p}}\max_{m\leq 2^{k}}|Y_{m}|=0\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

by the Borel-Cantelli lemma. ∎

We can now complete the proof of Corollary 3.32.

#### Proof of Corollary 3.32.

We prove both parts separately.

Part a. It suffices to verify that the assumptions of Theorem 3.29 are satisfied. Let $\mathrm{G}_{N}=([d_{N}],E_{N})$ be $k_{N}$ -regular, and write

$$ H_{k}^{N}=\sum_{i<j:\{i,j\}\in E_{N}}\frac{\eta_{kij}}{\sqrt{k_{N}}}(e_{i}e_{j}^{*}+e_{j}e_{i}^{*}). $$

Then $\mathbf{E}[H_{k}^{N}]=0$ and $\mathbf{E}[(H_{k}^{N})^{2}]=\mathbf{1}$ by construction. Furthermore, we have

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}(\log d_{N})^{\frac{3}{2}}v(H_{k}^{N})=\sqrt{2}\lim_{N\to\infty}(\log d_{N})^{\frac{3}{2}}k_{N}^{-\frac{1}{2}}=0 $$

by the assumption of part a. On the other hand, note that

$$ \mathbf{E}\bigg[\max_{1\leq i\leq M_{N}}\|Z_{ki}^{N}\|^{2}\bigg]\leq\frac{1}{k_{N}}\mathbf{E}\bigg[\max_{i<j:\{i,j\}\in E_{N}}|\eta_{kij}|^{p}\bigg]^{\frac{2}{p}}\leq\frac{(k_{N}d_{N})^{\frac{2}{p}}}{k_{N}}\mathbf{E}[|\eta_{kij}|^{p}]^{\frac{2}{p}}. $$

As the assumption of part a. implies $(k_{N}d_{N})^{\frac{2}{p}}k_{N}^{-1}\ll(\log d_{N})^{-4}$ , we have shown that $(\log d_{N})^{2}\bar{R}(H_{k}^{N})\to 0$ as $N\to\infty$ . This simultaneously verifies both remaining assumptions of the in probability version of Theorem 3.29.

If in addition $E_{N}$ is increasing, we can use Lemma 9.22 to obtain

$$ \limsup_{N\to\infty}\,(\log d_{N})^{2}\max_{1\leq i\leq M_{N}}\|Z_{ki}^{N}\|\lesssim\lim_{N\to\infty}(k_{N}d_{N})^{-\frac{1}{p}}\max_{i<j:\{i,j\}\in E_{N}}|\eta_{kij}|=0\quad\mbox{a.s.}, $$

where we used that $(\log d_{N})^{2}k_{N}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lesssim(k_{N}d_{N})^{-\frac{1}{p}}$ by the assumption of part a. The remaining conclusion of part a. then follows from the a.s. version of Theorem 3.29.

Part b. Fix any $p>2$ . Then we may choose a distribution of the entries $\eta_{kij}$ such that $\mathbf{E}[\eta_{kij}]=0$ , $\mathrm{Var}(\eta_{kij})=1$ , and $\mathbf{P}[|\eta_{kij}|>x]=(x\log x)^{-p}$ for all $x\geq x_{0}$ (here $x_{0}>0$ is a sufficiently large constant). As $\mathbf{E}[|\eta_{kij}|^{p}]<\infty$ , the assumptions of Corollary 3.32 are satisfied. Now note that as $\|M\|\geq\max_{i,j}|M_{ij}|$ , we have

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\|H_{1}^{N}\|>k_{N}^{-\frac{1}{2}}x\big]\geq\mathbf{P}\bigg[\max_{i<j:\{i,j\}\in E_{N}}|(H_{1}^{N})_{ij}|>k_{N}^{-\frac{1}{2}}x\bigg]=1-\big(1-(x\log x)^{-p}\big)^{\frac{k_{N}d_{N}}{2}} $$

for $x\geq x_{0}$ . Choosing $x=(k_{N}d_{N})^{\frac{1}{p}}(\log d_{N})^{-1}$ yields $(x\log x)^{-p}\geq(k_{N}d_{N})^{-1}$ for all sufficiently large $N$ , where we used $k_{N}\leq d_{N}$ . We have therefore shown that

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\|H_{1}^{N}\|>k_{N}^{\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}}d_{N}^{\frac{1}{p}}(\log d_{N})^{-1}\big]\geq 1-e^{-\frac{1}{2}} $$

for all large $N$ . But the assumption of part b. implies that $k_{N}^{\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}}d_{N}^{\frac{1}{p}}(\log d_{N})^{-1}\to\infty$ . This stands in contradiction to the conclusion of part a., which would imply in particular that $\|H_{1}^{N}\|\to\|s_{1}\|=2$ in probability. ∎

### 9.5. Phase transitions in spiked models

Here we prove Theorem 3.35. We first prove convergence of the outlier eigenvalues (as in part a. of Theorem 3.34), and then consider the eigenvectors (as in part b. of Theorem 3.34).

In the following, it will be convenient to introduce the notation

$$ \mathrm{B}(\theta):=\begin{cases}\theta+\frac{1}{\theta}&\mbox{for }\theta>1,\\
2&\mbox{for }\theta\leq 1,\end{cases} $$

and to write $\theta_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\theta_{s}>1\geq\theta_{s+1}\geq\cdots\geq\theta_{r}>0=:\theta_{r+1}$ . The assumptions of Theorem 3.35 will be assumed to hold without further comment.

#### 9.5.1. Outlier eigenvalues

We begin by a direct application of universality.

#### Lemma 9.23.

$\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(A_{d}+H_{d}),\mathrm{sp}(A_{d}+G_{d}))\to 0$ as $d\to\infty$ a.s.

#### Proof.

We readily compute $\sigma(A_{d}+H_{d})=O(1)$ and $\sigma_{*}(A_{d}+H_{d})=O(d^{-\frac{1}{2}})$ , while by assumption $R(A_{d}+H_{d})=o((\log d)^{-2})$ . Theorem 2.6 with $t=3\log d$ yields

$$ \mathbf{P}[\mathrm{d_{H}}(\mathrm{sp}(A_{d}+H_{d}),\mathrm{sp}(A_{d}+G_{d}))>o(1)]\leq\frac{1}{d^{2}}, $$

and the conclusion follows by the Borel-Cantelli lemma. ∎

When combined with Theorem 3.34, Lemma 9.23 suffices to detect the presence and locations of any outlier eigenvalues. However, Hausdorff convergence is not sufficiently strong to establish convergence of individual eigenvalues. In the present setting, this stronger conclusion can however be achieved by combining universality with the min-max principle. To this end we will use the following lemma.

#### Lemma 9.24.

Fix any orthonormal eigenvectors $v_{d,1},\ldots,v_{d,r}$ of $A_{d}$ with eigenvalues $\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{r}$ , respectively, and let $Q_{d,i}$ be the projection onto $\{v_{d,1},\ldots,v_{d,i}\}^{\perp}$ . Then $\lambda_{1}(Q_{d,i}(A_{d}+H_{d})Q_{d,i}^{*})\to\mathrm{B}(\theta_{i+1})$ as $d\to\infty$ a.s. for $i=1,\ldots,r$ .

#### Proof.

The identical argument as in Lemma 9.23 yields that

$$ |\lambda_{1}(Q_{d,i}(A_{d}+H_{d})Q_{d,i}^{*})-\lambda_{1}(Q_{d,i}(A_{d}+G_{d})Q_{d,i}^{*})|\xrightarrow{d\to\infty}0\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

But $Q_{d,i}G_{d}Q_{d,i}^{*}$ is GOE of dimension $d-i$ (scaled by a factor $(\frac{d-i}{d})^{\frac{1}{2}}=1+o(1)$ ). Thus applying Theorem 3.34 to $Q_{d,i}(A_{d}+G_{d})Q_{d,i}^{*}$ yields the conclusion. ∎

We can now deduce the convergence of the eigenvalues.

#### Corollary 9.25.

$\lambda_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\to\mathrm{B}(\theta_{i})$ as $d\to\infty$ a.s. for $1\leq i\leq r+1$ .

#### Proof.

Note first that $\lambda_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\leq\lambda_{1}(Q_{d,i-1}(A_{d}+H_{d})Q_{d,i-1}^{*})$ by the min-max principle. Thus $\limsup_{d\to\infty}\lambda_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\leq\mathrm{B}(\theta_{i})$ a.s. by Lemma 9.24.

Next, note that the empirical spectral distribution of $H_{d}$ converges a.s. to the standard semicircle distribution by Theorem 3.29. This implies in particular that $\liminf_{d\to\infty}\lambda_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\geq\liminf_{d\to\infty}\lambda_{i}(H_{d})\geq 2$ a.s. for all $1\leq i\leq r+1$ . Thus we obtain $\lambda_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\to\mathrm{B}(\theta_{i})=2$ as $d\to\infty$ a.s. for $s+1\leq i\leq r+1$ .

On the other hand, by Lemma 9.23 and Theorem 3.34, each $\mathrm{B}(\theta_{i})$ with $1\leq i\leq s$ is a limit point of the spectrum of $A_{d}+H_{d}$ as $d\to\infty$ . If $\theta_{1}>\theta_{2}>\cdots>\theta_{s}$ are all distinct, this immediately implies $\liminf_{d\to\infty}\lambda_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\geq\mathrm{B}(\theta_{i})$ a.s., concluding the proof. If $\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{s}$ are not distinct, we can choose $0\leq A_{d}^{\prime}\leq A_{d}$ of rank $r$ with distinct nonzero eigenvalues so that $\lambda_{i}(A_{d}^{\prime})\geq\theta_{i}-\varepsilon$ for all $1\leq i\leq r$ . Then

$$ \liminf_{d\to\infty}\lambda_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\geq\liminf_{d\to\infty}\lambda_{i}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d})\geq\mathrm{B}(\theta_{i}-\varepsilon)\quad\mbox{a.s.}, $$

and the conclusion follows as $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary. ∎

#### 9.5.2. Outlier eigenvectors

A universality statement for eigenvectors of $A_{d}+H_{d}$ can be obtained using Theorem 2.10. This yields the following conclusion.

#### Lemma 9.26.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ be sufficiently small that $I_{i}:=\theta_{i}+\frac{1}{\theta_{i}}+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ are disjoint for distinct values of $\theta_{i}$ . Then for all $1\leq i\leq s$ and nonrandom $v_{d}\in\mathbb{C}^{d}$ , $\|v_{d}\|=1$

$$ |\langle v_{d},1_{I_{i}}(A_{d}+H_{d})v_{d}\rangle-\langle v_{d},1_{I_{i}}(A_{d}+G_{d})v_{d}\rangle|\xrightarrow{d\to\infty}0\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

#### Proof.

Let $\varphi_{i}:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ be a smooth function so that $\varphi_{i}(x)=0$ for $x\not\in I_{i}$ and $\varphi_{i}(x)=1$ for $x\in\theta_{i}+\frac{1}{\theta_{i}}+[-\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\varepsilon}{2}]$ . Then the second part of Theorem 2.10 yields

$$ |\mathbf{E}[\langle v_{d},\varphi_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})v_{d}\rangle]-\mathbf{E}[\langle v_{d},\varphi_{i}(A_{d}+G_{d})v_{d}\rangle]|\xrightarrow{d\to\infty}0. $$

On the other hand, applying Proposition 5.10 with $x=2C^{-1}\log d$ yields

$$ \mathbf{P}\big[\big|\langle v_{d},\varphi_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})v_{d}\rangle-\mathbf{E}[\langle v_{d},\varphi_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})v_{d}\rangle]\big|\geq o(1)\big]\leq\frac{4}{d^{2}}, $$

and analogously for $A_{d}+G_{d}$ . Thus the Borel-Cantelli lemma yields

$$ |\langle v_{d},\varphi_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})v_{d}\rangle-\langle v_{d},\varphi_{i}(A_{d}+G_{d})v_{d}\rangle|\xrightarrow{d\to\infty}0\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

But $\varphi_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})=1_{I_{i}}(A_{d}+H_{d})$ and $\varphi_{i}(A_{d}+G_{d})=1_{I_{i}}(A_{d}+G_{d})$ eventually as $d\to\infty$ a.s. by Corollary 9.25 and by part a. of Theorem 3.34, respectively. ∎

The desired properties of the eigenvectors now follow directly in the case that $\theta_{1}>\cdots>\theta_{s}$ are all distinct. The main difficulty is to remove the latter requirement by means of a suitable perturbation argument.

#### Corollary 9.27.

For any $1\leq i\leq s$ and $1\leq j\leq r$ , we have

$$ \|P_{j}(A_{d})v_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\|^{2}\xrightarrow[\text{a.s.}]{d\to\infty}\bigg(1-\frac{1}{\theta_{i}^{2}}\bigg)1_{\theta_{j}=\theta_{i}}. $$

#### Proof.

If $\theta_{1}>\cdots>\theta_{s}$ are all distinct, then $1_{I_{i}}(A_{d}+H_{d})=v_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})v_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})^{*}$ and $1_{I_{i}}(A_{d}+G_{d})=v_{i}(A_{d}+G_{d})v_{i}(A_{d}+G_{d})^{*}$ eventually as $d\to\infty$ a.s. for $1\leq i\leq s$ by Corollary 9.25 and part a. of Theorem 3.34. The conclusion then follows readily by applying Lemma 9.26 and part b. of Theorem 3.34.

In the general case, let $A_{d}^{\prime}=\sum_{m=1}^{r}\theta_{m}^{\prime}\,v_{m}(A_{d})v_{m}(A_{d})^{*}$ be a perturbation of $A_{d}$ (for a choice of orthonormal eigenvectors $v_{m}(A_{d})$ ) with distinct $\theta_{1}^{\prime}>\cdots>\theta_{r}^{\prime}$ and such that $|\theta_{m}-\theta_{m}^{\prime}|\leq\varepsilon$ for all $m$ . Let $J_{i}:=\{k:\theta_{k}=\theta_{i}\}$ , and let $Q_{i}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d})$ be the projection on the linear span of $\{v_{k}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d}):k\in J_{i}\}$ . We claim that

$$ \limsup_{d\to\infty}\bigg|\|P_{j}(A_{d})\tilde{v}_{d,i}\|^{2}-\bigg(1-\frac{1}{\theta_{i}^{2}}\bigg)1_{\theta_{j}=\theta_{i}}\bigg|\lesssim\varepsilon\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

for any (possibly random) choice of unit vector $\tilde{v}_{d,i}\in\mathop{\mathrm{ran}}(Q_{i}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d}))$ . Indeed, writing $\tilde{v}_{d,i}=\sum_{k\in J_{i}}c_{d,k}v_{k}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d})$ with $\sum_{k\in J_{i}}c_{d,k}^{2}=1$ , we can compute

$$ \displaystyle\|P_{j}(A_{d})\tilde{v}_{d,i}\|^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{m\in J_{j}}\sum_{k,l\in J_{i}}c_{d,k}c_{d,l}\langle v_{k}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d}),v_{m}(A_{d})\rangle\langle v_{m}(A_{d}),v_{l}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d})\rangle \displaystyle=\sum_{k\in J_{i}}c_{d,k}^{2}\bigg(1-\frac{1}{(\theta_{k}^{\prime})^{2}}\bigg)1_{\theta_{j}=\theta_{i}}+o(1)\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

as $d\to\infty$ , where we used that $|\langle v_{m}(A_{d}),v_{l}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d})\rangle|^{2}\to(1-\frac{1}{(\theta_{l}^{\prime})^{2}})1_{m=l}$ a.s. as $A_{d}^{\prime}$ has distinct eigenvalues. The claim follows as $\theta\mapsto 1-\frac{1}{\theta^{2}}$ is Lipschitz on $[1,\infty)$ .

For any projection matrices $P,Q\in\mathrm{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$ , we can write

$$ \sup_{v\in\mathop{\mathrm{ran}}Q,\|v\|=1}\big|\|Pv\|^{2}-c\,\big|=\|Q(P-c\mathbf{1})Q\|. $$

Using this identity, the above claim may be rewritten as

$$ \limsup_{d\to\infty}\big\|Q_{i}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d})\big(P_{j}(A_{d})-(\textstyle{1-\frac{1}{\theta_{i}^{2}}})1_{\theta_{j}=\theta_{i}}\mathbf{1}\big)Q_{i}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d})\big\|\lesssim\varepsilon\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

On the other hand, when $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small, Corollary 9.25 ensures that the eigenvalues $\{\lambda_{k}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d}):k\in J_{i}\}$ are separated from the rest of the spectrum of $A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d}$ by a positive gap as $d\to\infty$ . A routine application of the Davis-Kahan theorem [18, Theorem VII.3.1 and Exercise VII.1.11] yields

$$ \|Q_{i}(A_{d}^{\prime}+H_{d})-Q_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\|\lesssim\|A_{d}^{\prime}-A_{d}\|\leq\varepsilon $$

eventually as $d\to\infty$ a.s. As we may choose $\varepsilon>0$ arbitrarily small, it follows that

$$ \big\|Q_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\big(P_{j}(A_{d})-(\textstyle{1-\frac{1}{\theta_{i}^{2}}})1_{\theta_{j}=\theta_{i}}\mathbf{1}\big)Q_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\big\|\xrightarrow{d\to\infty}0\quad\mbox{a.s.} $$

The conclusion follows as $v_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d})\in\mathop{\mathrm{ran}}(Q_{i}(A_{d}+H_{d}))$ . ∎

Combining Corollaries 9.25 and 9.27 concludes the proof of Theorem 3.35.
